stories.title: Karabell's notebook: Murray's hot start, Adebayo's struggles, other early trends
stories.summary: Eric Karabell empties out the notebook with all that he's noticing around the NBA, and what it means for fantasy.
stories.detailText: I don't think many people recall that SG/PG Dejounte Murray once averaged 21.1 PPG, 8.3 RPG, 9.2 APG and 2.0 SPG for the 2021-22 San Antonio Spurs . Those numbers were outrageous! Yeah, we knew he would not be able to replicate those numbers the following season with PG Trae Young 's immense usage in Atlanta, but Murray was still very good there. Then he went to the New Orleans Pelicans and was doing fine -- until he tore his Achilles. He played 45 games during his first two Pelicans seasons. Did fantasy managers forget the good times, or overlook them a bit? It's early in the 2026-27 season, but Murray is back to being a modest fantasy building block, averaging 20.3 PPG, 5.0 RPG and 6.3 APG -- with 2.3 SPG and 1.3 BPG! -- for a terrible team. His usage is back and the numbers are outstanding (though the block rate cannot continue). Most fantasy managers did not see this coming. I saw Murray's name mentioned as a potential bust, because he didn't shoot all that much when he finally debuted for his 14 appearances last season, and he was turning 30, and it's tough to thrive after a torn Achilles and, well, just stop it ... Murray is thriving, despite the relative mess around him, and I particularly love the percentages: 49% FG and 88.9% FT is so valuable, regardless of format. This has always been an underrated player, for fantasy purposes and otherwise. Perhaps he cannot earn his second career All-Star nod if the Pelicans never win, but fantasy managers will love him, especially those who didn't need to invest a top-60 selection on draft day to get him. I grabbed Murray in Round 1 of a keeper league (each team kept four players), and I am glad I did. Other observations around the NBA My fantasy hoops preference is roto/categories formats, so I tend to love the versatile statistical options who pile on both rebounds and assists while not killing the shooting percentages. It's why I can't get enough of Hawks PF Jalen Johnson , who is averaging a near-triple double. Chicago Bulls PG Josh Giddey won't shoot 33.3% from the field for long, right? I see you, Orlando Magic SF/PF Franz Wagner and Brooklyn Nets PF Julius Randle . Speaking of the Magic, now without PF/SF Paolo Banchero and PG/SG Jalen Suggs , go add PG/SG Anthony Black . He missed the first two games with an ankle sprain and then scored 18 points in 26 minutes Sunday. He won't drain five 3-pointers every game, but Black showed glimpses of fantasy stardom filling in for injured players last season. He averaged 18.2 PPG, 5.0 RPG and 5.0 APG during December/January games. The Magic must give him minutes now, and this is a good thing. Is it me or are the turnovers way up so far? (It's not just me. Entering Tuesday, teams were averaging 16.6 TPG. That number was 14.5 TPG last season!) Regardless, this affects fantasy managers in points formats, or in roto leagues that count turnovers, as one of mine does. We have a stat for assist-turnover ratio. LA Clippers PG Darius Garland , one of "my guys" this season , is averaging 7.0 APG and 6.0 TPG so far. Yeah, that's more James Harden -like than we want, and it is not really going to work. The non-related George brothers ( Kyshawn George of Washington, Keyonte George from Utah) are both way up there. Nobody cares that Luka Doncic had an 11-turnover game because he scored 52 points two nights later. Anyway, I am sure the turnover trend will normalize some, but I am watching this. The Detroit Pistons didn't need a healthy C Jalen Duren (hamstring) to beat the Philadelphia 76ers on Sunday night, because the 76ers have no interior presence when C Joel Embiid sits. And Embiid is going to sit a lot, and not merely in back-to-back situations. SF/PF LeBron James logged center minutes Sunday, and afterward he told reporters he didn't like it. Awesome! Look, the 76ers weren't going to win every game , but they desperately need more rebounding. James is averaging 16.3 PPG so far thanks to poor shooting (42.9% FG, 63.2% FT), but I expect more like 18 PPG. It will improve. I still think James appears in more than 65 games this season. Now feels like a good time to trade for him. I really don't care whether 76ers SF/SG Jaylen Brown and former Boston Celtics teammate PF/SF Jayson Tatum like each other or not. Many people who work together aren't pals, you know, so why would they be pals later? What a silly story. I care that Brown missed 15 of 20 shots on Sunday, but we must view that outing as aberrant. The Pistons defend well. The 76ers play them again only two more times. Brown and PG/SG Tyrese Maxey are both averaging a ton of minutes so far, and fantasy managers should embrace it. Maxey is the clear star here, but Brown can average roughly 24-25 PPG this season, too. It's way too early to worry about top 50 players from drafts, but I can say if drafting again, Miami Heat C/PF Bam Adebayo would not be in my top 50. He is averaging 11.8 PPG, 7.3 RPG and shooting 40% FG through four games, and what's up with the 61.5% FT? It just feels like a clunky fit with newcomer PF/C Giannis Antetokounmpo . Adebayo will improve his shooting, but I doubt he averages close to 20 PPG or 10 RPG like last season. Miami's offense finally ran through Giannis on Monday, when he had 11 assists. He had nine total in the first three games. PG Davion Mitchell , who had 26 assists in three games, delivered only two on Monday. Ah, I liked Mitchell. Oh well, that's over. It's all Giannis, and the Heat remain winless. Nobody expected much from the Sacramento Kings , of course, but two things stand out so far, and neither has anything to do with SG/SF Zach LaVine , who can't average 29 PPG for long (you have been warned). One is that C/PF Domantas Sabonis looks awesome, and my preseason prediction of him winning his fourth rebounding title in five seasons is off to a solid start. The other thing to watch is rookie PG Darius Acuff Jr . , because the volume of missed shots is staggering. Acuff is shooting 32.9% through three games and a brutal 14.8% from 3-point range. I don't see him piling on the assists in an offense run by Sabonis, but he must shoot better than this or fantasy managers cannot count on him. Keep an eye on Memphis Grizzlies SF/SG Cedric Coward this week. Coward missed Friday's game with the Golden State Warriors with a wrist injury, got dropped by some leagues, and then he delivered double-doubles Sunday and Monday. I think a real star lurks here, that he ultimately leads the Grizzles in scoring at like 18 PPG. I mean, good for PG Ty Jerome so far, but 29.8 PPG is wild. Coward is the future star here and remains available in more than 57% of ESPN leagues. Get him!

stories.title: Jazz's Jaren Jackson Jr. (knee) out 6-8 weeks, sources say
stories.summary: Utah will be down two more of its bigs as Jaren Jackson Jr. has a torn MCL in his right knee and will miss at least six weeks, while Lauri Markkanen is day-to-day with a sprained wrist.
stories.detailText: Utah Jazz star power forward/center Jaren Jackson Jr . has sustained a torn MCL in his right knee and will be reevaluated in six weeks, the team announced Tuesday. Sources told ESPN that Jackson is looking at a six- to eight-week timetable to return from the injury he suffered Monday night. The Jazz also announced that Lauri Markkanen is day-to-day with a sprained right wrist. He also exited Monday's home loss to the Memphis Grizzlies in the first half with the injury. Utah is hopeful that 7-foot Markkanen won't miss an extended period, but the injury is to his shooting wrist, which is particularly problematic for a volume 3-point shooter. Jackson, a two-time All-Star and 2023 Defensive Player of the Year acquired in a blockbuster deal before last season's trade deadline, was injured when Grizzles guard Ty Jerome fell into him and caused his knee to buckle. Jackson played only three games for the Jazz last season after the trade before undergoing surgery to remove a noncancerous growth in his left knee. Utah sent three first-round picks to the Grizzlies in the deal, which Jazz management hoped would fuel the franchise's return to competitiveness this season. The Jazz's frontcourt has been devastated by injuries. Starting center Jusuf Nurkic has yet to play this season due to a partial plantar plate tear of the second toe in his right foot, an injury that is scheduled to be reevaluated in early November.

stories.title: Where does Oklahoma City go from here?
stories.summary: More Ajay Mitchell plus a deep roster means OKC will win a lot of regular season games. But the playoffs...
stories.detailText: It was a devastating 24 hours in Oklahoma City. Everyone who saw Jalen Williams go down against the Clippers knew how bad it was, as Thunder GM Sam Presti put it, "This is an injury that generally we see more in football players." On top of that came the news that Cason Wallace has a torn labrum and will need to undergo surgery. Presti and OKC won't put a timeline on things, but history suggests neither player will touch the court again this season. Now what? What should we expect from the Thunder going forward? First: Expect a lot of wins. This team was without Williams for large chunks of last regular season and still won 64 games, most in the NBA. In their one game so far without their two starters (not to mention no Chet Holmgren or Alex Caruso), the Thunder still easily handled the Suns. The other change is that while the defense will still be good, it will not be elite. Instead, this is about to become an offensive team. That wins a lot of regular-season games. But what about the playoffs? And what should we look for? More Ajay Mitchell, Jared McCain The Thunder have a natural replacement for Wallace: Ajay Mitchell. In his first game in that role this season, Mitchell stepped up, showed off his physicality and midrange game, and dropped 30 on the Suns. Ajay Mitchell STARRED in OKC's victory! 30 PTS (career-high) 5 AST 10-16 FGM The Thunder improve to 4-0 on the season pic.twitter.com/vOuhpDoddo — NBA (@NBA) October 27, 2026 Mitchell is not the All-Defense-level player on that end that Wallace is, but he works hard and is a plus defender who fits within the system. Williams is a more difficult role to fill, largely because there aren't other players like him. There will be more Alex Caruso, but coach Mark Daigneault and the Thunder know they can't overtax him. Jared McCain will get more minutes, but he is a guard, not a forward. Kenrich Williams may see the biggest jump in minutes, and he is rock solid, but he's not an All-NBA level talent like Williams. Lean into center rotation Oklahoma City has the best big man rotation in the NBA. Chet Holmgren — second in Defensive Player of the Year voting last season while averaging 17.1 points per game — and Isaiah Hartenstein start at the four and five. However, what makes this work is the depth. Jaylin Williams is the kind of big off the bench every team could use, and rookie Aday Mara has proven he deserves a spot in the rotation. Aday Mara MAKING PLAYS in his first NBA game Big-time swat at the rim. Two-hand alley-oop slam. The Thunder lead in Q3! pic.twitter.com/YJpmoBAm8J — NBA (@NBA) October 21, 2026 Oklahoma City needs to lean hard into its strengths, and it has the best center rotation in the league. Don’t expect big trade When asked about what the injuries mean in terms of a roster move, Thunder General Manager Sam Presti said he hadn't thought about that yet. He was still processing the injuries. However, the tea leaves suggest OKC is not likely to make a big move. First, this team is already good, has great locker-room chemistry and wins games. Why mess with that? Second, this team made moves this offseason that Presti admitted weren't basketball moves but were about saving money, trading away Lu Dort, Aaron Wiggins and Isaiah Joe. As constructed, the Thunder are expensive and about to get even more so in the coming years. Oklahoma City is already over the first apron of the luxury tax and is about $6.9 million below the second apron, a line they are very unlikely to cross during the season. While the Thunder have an open roster spot and can get a disabled player exception for Williams worth close to $15 million, no game-changing free agents are available for them to snap up. The Thunder could consider a trade depending on how the season plays out, but they don't want to mess up their chemistry or take on much more money. The Thunder are going to stick with the players they have, and at the trade deadline they can make small adjustments as needed, but it's far more likely to be small moves, not a blockbuster. What does all this mean for the Thunder in the playoffs? It's far too early to have a clear picture of the West, but Oklahoma City has gone from the early favorite in the West to a team that will enter the playoffs with matchups in mind. Who do they have now who can defend Luka Doncic or Kevin Durant? The road for the Thunder back to the NBA Finals just got bumpier and steeper, but it's not closed off. Things will look different, but OKC could still win it all.

stories.title: Hornets to retire Muggsy Bogues' No. 1 jersey
stories.summary: The Hornets will retire Muggsy Bogues' No. 1 jersey on Feb. 11. Bogues, the shortest player in NBA history, is the franchise leader in assists, steals and minutes.
stories.detailText: The Charlotte Hornets are retiring the No. 1 jersey of Muggsy Bogues, the shortest player in NBA history, on Feb. 11. The 5-foot-3 Bogues spent 10 of his 14 NBA seasons in Charlotte (1988-1998) and is the franchise leader in assists, steals and minutes. "How ironic is that?" Bogues said. "After all those times that you felt like you were looking up, looking up for so many years, at people. Then here comes this particular moment, and when that jersey actually goes up it'll be like I'm the one looking down at the entire world. It's going to be a surreal moment." Bogues, 61, has spent more than 20 years with the Hornets as a player and ambassador after initially joining the franchise in the 1988 expansion draft. "Charlotte embraced me with open arms," Bogues said. "This is a place I've called home more than I've called any other place home, even growing up in the city of Baltimore. So, having this type of recognition for my family, for the organization to look at you in this type of light, I mean, it means the world." Hornets owners Rick Schnall and Gabe Plotkin made the decision to retire Bogues' No. 1 to continue the organization's connectivity with its history and legends. "I was just like any kid that had a dream," Bogues said. "I just kept believing and kept having success. And my mindset was, 'If you play against the best, and you have success against the best, you need to be included with the best.'" Bogues joins Bobby Phills (No. 13) and Dell Curry (No. 30) as the only players to have their jerseys retired for the Hornets.

stories.title: Ex-NBA guard Malik Beasley to plead guilty after involvement in gambling scheme
stories.summary: Malik Beasley was indicted in June after prosecutors said he manipulated several NBA games in a larger gambling scheme.
stories.detailText: Longtime former NBA guard Malik Beasley has agreed to plead guilty to federal charges related to illegal sports gambling, his attorney told both The Athletic and ESPN on Tuesday. Beasley, who was arrested earlier this summer, will officially enter his plea Dec. 9 in New York. Beasley was indicted in June on federal charges related to a sports betting scheme alongside former NBA veteran Ed Davis. The duo, who played together for the Minnesota Timberwolves, were accused of working together to manipulate Beasley's performance in four games during the 2023-24 campaign. Beasley was on the Milwaukee Bucks at the time, and Davis was out of the league. Beasley reportedly owed millions of dollars in a gambling debt, which led to Davis loaning Beasley money. But in order to pay off that debt, Beasley and Davis reportedly decided to launch a betting scheme. They allegedly worked with three others to place tens of thousands of dollars on a game that Beasley played in against the Cleveland Cavaliers that season. Beasley ended up scoring just three points in that game, well below his season average of 11.3 points per contest. Beasley is also accused of rigging a game against the Charlotte Hornets in similar fashion that same season. Beasley has not played in the league since the 2024-25 season, which was one of the best in his career. He averaged 16.3 points per game, his best output in years, and finished second in the Sixth Man of the Year race while with the Detroit Pistons. He was due for a big payday after that season, too, but his free agency was interrupted both by a federal gambling investigation and an NBA investigation into Beasley. He went unsigned and hasn't played since. Prosecutors alleged that Davis was in charge of the scheme. They were two of six men indicted in the scheme. Beasley is the second active NBA player to plead guilty to charges related to gambling in the NBA. Jontay Porter was the first and pleaded guilty in July 2024 amid a separate but similar scheme. The NBA banned him for life in 2024 . It's unclear if Beasley will face that same fate.

stories.title: Bam Adebayo feels like the 'scapegoat' amid struggles, Heat's 0-4 start to the season
stories.summary: The Dallas Mavericks beat Miami 113-109 on Monday night despite a triple-double from new Heat star Giannis Antetokounmpo.
stories.detailText: Bam Adebayo is not OK with taking the blame for the Miami Heat's brutal 0-4 start to the season. The Heat star, after the team fell 113-109 to the Dallas Mavericks on Monday night, said he feels singled out for the franchise's struggles — especially after it landed Giannis Antetokounmpo in a blockbuster deal this past offseason. "You know, it's funny how the outside noise wants to make me the scapegoat," Adebayo said, via ESPN . "But when the tables turn, just all that energy, when the energy shifts, just be prepared for that." Though it's not fair to put all of the blame on Adebayo, he has struggled in the early stretch of the season. Adebayo is averaging just 11.8 points and 7.3 rebounds per game, and is only shooting 16.7% from the 3-point line. He had just eight points and went 3-of-10 on Monday night, and missed all five of his attempts from behind the arc. Antetokounmpo, meanwhile, had a triple-double with 29 points, 14 rebounds and 11 assists. By comparison, Adebayo averaged 20.1 points and 10 rebounds per game last season. He even dropped 83 points in a single game in March, which is the second-most scored by a player in a single contest in NBA history. Only Wilt Chamberlain's 100-point game in 1962 sits ahead of him on that list. For now, Adebayo said his struggles are simply because his shot is not going in. It's nothing more. "I got expectations for myself, but, obviously, the outside noise got expectations for us," he said. "So for me, I know what I'm capable of. I'm not going to overthink that. We're 0-4 right now. I'd rather it be right now than this be midway through the season or in April. Because what if we go on a 10-game winning streak? Then how does the noise change?" The Heat will take on the Atlanta Hawks next on Wednesday. A loss there would match their worst start since the 2007-08 campaign. The Heat also currently hold the worst record in the league, though four other franchises are also still searching for their first wins. Miami still has time to figure out how all the pieces work together now that Antetokounmpo is in the mix. Bam's numbers falling from last season seemed inevitable after the trade. But so far, it's not been a good start. "It's not just Bam, it's everybody," Antetokounmpo said. "You know, everybody — we try to figure out where we fit in and what we gotta do. Kind of try to not step on our toes."

stories.detailText: Utah Jazz center Jaren Jackson Jr. has a torn MCL in his right knee and will miss at least six weeks. The Jazz announced Jackson's diagnosis Tuesday after he sustained the injury Monday night in a 110-105 loss to the Memphis Grizzlies . Jackson isn't expected to undergo surgery. Former All-Star Lauri Markkanen also left Monday's game with a wrist injury. The Jazz announced Tuesday that he has a sprained right wrist and is considered day-to-day. Tough blow for promising Jazz A two-time All-Star and former Defensive Player of the Year, Jackson is a centerpiece of a revamped Jazz roster that hopes to compete for a playoff spot this season after four straight years of missing the postseason. The Jazz acquired Jackson from the Grizzlies at last season's trade deadline, signaling their intent to return to competitiveness this season amid a 22-60 campaign that secured the No. 2 pick in the draft and the rights to select Darryn Peterson. Jackson had surgery on his right knee shortly after joining the Jazz to remove a non-cancerous pigmented villonodular synovitis growth in his left knee. He played just three games in his first season with the Jazz and will now be sidelined for a significant portion of the season. Jackson's injury occurred when Memphis guard Ty Jerome fell into his right leg after driving to the basket. Jackson's knee buckled, and he fell to the court in pain. The injuries to Jackson and Markkanen compound an already disappointing start to Utah's season. Tuesday's loss dropped the Jazz to 1-3. They're scheduled to face the reigning Western Conference champion Spurs in two of their next three games with a matchup against the 2-0 Trail Blazers in between. Markkanen's status for those games is unclear. When healthy, the Jazz feature a promising core of Jackson, Markkanen, Peterson, standout point guard Keyonte George and Ace Bailey, the No. 5 pick in the 2025 NBA Draft. Jaxson Hayes and Mo Bamba project to take on the bulk of Jackson's minutes at center, while Bailey and Peterson could see more opportunities in Utah's offense while Jackson and Markkanen are out.

stories.title: How Walker Kessler is anchoring the Lakers defense
stories.summary: It’s only been three games, but Walker Kessler has already proven himself a force on the defensive end for the Lakers.
stories.detailText: LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA - OCTOBER 23: Walker Kessler #14 of the Los Angeles Lakers defends during the game against the LA Clippers at Crypto.com Arena on October 23, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Ben Liebenberg/Getty Images) | Getty Images It took overcoming an 18-point deficit, but the Lakers remained 3-0 with Sunday’s road win over the Utah Jazz, led by Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves combining for 81 points. ​LA’s major offseason addition, Walker Kessler, struggled to contribute offensively as Utah game-planned to overload the paint. He finished 1-2 from the field for two points with seven rebounds and a block. Still, the former Jazz big man ended the night with a plus-minus of plus-six. ​While the return to Utah was quiet offensively, his first two games in the purple and gold were anything but. Kessler finished lobs and dump-off passes near the rim to average 24 points per night in those contests. ​His scoring consistency will fluctuate throughout the season, but the Lakers traded for him to be a defensive anchor every night and he’s immediately been a force on that end. Over three games, the Lakers have a 105.6 defensive rating with Kessler on the court, which would be good for sixth overall, along with a +26 net rating. ​The team’s entire defense hinges on his ability to protect the basket. The Lakers prefer to keep him in a drop coverage scheme, where he engages the ball handler enough for his teammate to chase over and recover, without letting his man roll behind. ​Kessler has a quick-twitch jump and elite mobility for his size, allowing him to react timely to offensive players. Watch below as Kris Dunn rejects the ball screen and heads to the rim. Kessler is in position to dissuade the pass to the big man while easily rejecting Dunn at the basket. While the Lakers would love to park Kessler near the rim at all times, that’s not how the modern game works. With the volume of screen actions every play and five-out offenses around the league, an elite big man must be able to defend the perimeter and still recover to the rim, sometimes multiple times per possession. The counter against a drop coverage is ball handlers with a pull-up jump shot, especially on 3-pointers. Against the Clippers and Darius Garland, Kessler was asked to meet the screen at the level to hedge the ball handler, as shown below, and recover to his man. Watch as he forces the ball out of Garland’s hands and still recovers to block Rui Hachimura at the basket. Kessler leads the Lakers in rebounds, is tied for second in the league in blocks and leads the team in 3-point contests per game. Head coach JJ Redick, at his opening media availability, noted he hopes to use Kessler similarly to how the Spurs use Victor Wembanyama. ​It’s a strategy where you start a rim protector on a less dangerous corner shooter. There’s a trust that he can protect the rim while recovering out enough in time to closeout effectively. Watch below as Kessler not only gets back in time to contest, but erases the rookie Keaton Wagler’s shot entirely. Kessler’s mere presence taps into the strengths of the defensive talent on the roster. LA signed two-time All-Defensive player Matisse Thybulle and young, athletic wing Ziaire Williams to be perimeter pests. ​He lets them be ultra-aggressive, knowing he’s flanking behind them. Watch as Thybulle chases over and takes multiple swipes at the ball against Draymond Green. If he’s out of position, Kessler is there to hinder any attack on the basket. While the Lakers haven’t played a row of contenders to start the season, roles have been clearly defined throughout the team. For Kessler, that’s been just as crystallized as everyone else. His job is to maintain his defensive motor and focus for every minute he plays. With his offensive responsibilities set to be a play finisher, he can save energy for the other side of the floor. ​There’s still a long way to go this season, but so far Kessler has answered the bell on what he was brought here to do. ​ You can follow Raj on X at @RajChipalu

stories.title: Muggsy Bogues will have his No. 1 jersey retired by Hornets in February
stories.summary: The team will honor the franchise legend before a February game against the Bucks.
stories.detailText: Muggsy Bogues will have his No. 1 jersey retired by the Charlotte Hornets in a halftime ceremony during their game against the Milwaukee Bucks on Feb. 11, 2027, the team announced on Tuesday . "Charlotte has been home to me and my family for so many years, and the support I've received from Hornets fans has meant everything to me," said Bogues in a statement. "To have my number retired alongside Bobby and Dell is an incredible honor. I'm grateful to [Co-Chairmen] Rick [Schnall] and Gabe [Plotkin], the organization, my teammates and coaches, and everyone who has been part of this journey. I can't wait to share this night with my family and the fans who have been with us since the beginning." Bogues, the shortest player in NBA history at 5-foot-3, spent parts of 10 seasons with the Hornets during his 14-year NBA career. He also played for the Washington Bullets, which drafted him 12th overall in 1987, as well as the Golden State Warriors and Toronto Raptors. on february 11th, we will honor the one & only muggsy bogues. 🐝 press release: https://t.co/gq6cYbwKM9 | @MuggsyBogues pic.twitter.com/jJ8zkefsWq — Charlotte Hornets (@hornets) October 27, 2026 After last playing during the 2000-01 season, Bogues retired as the Hornets' franchise leader in assists, steals and minutes played. During his time in Charlotte, he, along with Alonzo Mourning and Larry Johnson, became faces of a team that made the playoffs three times and won 54 games in 1996-97. Over 25 years since he last played, the 61-year-old Bogues now serves as an ambassador for the Hornets and the NBA. In March, when asked by the Charlotte Observer about what it would mean if the Hornets retired his No. 1, Bogues said he did not "need it to go up" and that he was "happy." "I don't need it to go up. That's good. I'm good. I'm fine with it," Bogues said after the Hornets retired Dell Curry's number . "I'm just happy for my guy, Dell, for him to get his recognition. That is definitely well deserved. I'm fine. You know, the organization doesn't have to do anything with me at all. Right now, I'm not looking down that road. They don't have to think about me in that way. I'm just happy, you know, for my brother from another mother." Bogues was all smiles when posing with his jersey alongside Curry after Tuesday’s announcement. one to the rafters. congrats, muggsy 🩵 pic.twitter.com/wRnTjqb7rz — Charlotte Hornets (@hornets) October 27, 2026 Bogues' No. 1 will join Curry's No. 30 and Bobby Phills' No. 13 as the only player numbers to have been given the honor by the Hornets.

Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Gary Dineen/NBAE via Getty Images). | NBAE via Getty Images The Los Angeles Lakers have opened the 2026-27 NBA season with Arthur Kaluma, Chris Mañon and AK Okereke occupying their trio of two-way contract spots. But according to Marc Stein and Jake Fischer , Los Angeles was intrigued by the possibility of adding Pete Nance on a two-way deal when Nance was a free agent earlier this month. “The 76ers and Lakers, league sources say, both registered two-way contract interest in Pete Nance after Milwaukee released the 26-year-old last weekend,“ Stein and Fischer reported. ”But the Bucks, as The Stein Line reported last Sunday, believed they could get Nance to stay in Brewtown on a two-way with them and were proven correct. Nance is still a Buck.“ Since going undrafted in 2023, Nance — the younger brother of former Laker Larry Nance Jr. — has spent time with the Bucks, Sixers and Cleveland Cavaliers. As Milwaukee labored through a lost season last year, Nance received the most run of his brief career thus far. He played in a career-high 47 games, logged a career-high 737 minutes and averaged a career-high 5.4 points per game, headlined by a 23-point outing against the Houston Rockets and 11 other double-digit scoring nights. Nance’s standout trait is seemingly his outside shooting, having drained 41.7% of his career triples (60-of-144). While he wouldn’t have presumably factored into the Lakers’ rotation , that floor-spacing as a legit 4 could’ve provided a nice duplicative element behind Sandro Mamukelashvili in times of rotational crisis. For now, though, he remains with the Bucks while the Lakers roll with Kaluma, Mañon and Okereke. Among the three, only Mañon’s logged regular-season minutes (three) to this point, with two of the Lakers’ three wins being undecided until late in the fourth quarter. Most of their playing time will likely come with the South Bay Lakers in the G League, which begins its season Nov. 6 with the Tip-Off Tournament. Both Kaluma and Mañon played for South Bay last season while Okereke is a rookie. In 35 regular-season appearances, Kaluma averaged 14.6 points, 5.0 rebounds and 1.6 assists, and shot 54.5% from the floor (36.4% beyond the arc). Mañon made 33 appearances, averaging 10.3 points, 5.6 rebounds, 2.2 assists and 2.0 steals. You can follow Jackson on Twitter at @jackfrank_jjf .

stories.title: Dynasty Basketball Stock Watch: Ty Jerome, Leonard Miller rising, uncertainty for Jalen Williams
stories.summary: Tracking the biggest risers, fallers and emerging prospects in dynasty fantasy basketball leagues.
stories.detailText: The 2026-27 NBA season has kicked off, and we already have some fun things to break down. We had the 76ers spoil the Knicks’ good vibes on Opening Night before they came back from 29 points down to beat the Cleveland Cavaliers. We've had the Miami Heat struggle out of the gate, and the Timberwolves look amazing. Among the early headlines, there's been some impressive fantasy performances and dynasty value implications. Let's break down two risers and two fallers this past week before looking ahead to some NBA Draft prospects. Fantasy Basketball Top 200 Rankings: Critical injuries and Ty Jerome’s red-hot Week 1 The latest top-200 fantasy basketball rankings, with a surprising name leading the way. Raphielle Johnson , Dynasty Risers of the Week Ty Jerome, Memphis Grizzlies After breaking out in 2024-25, Ty Jerome signed with the Grizzlies in the 2025 offseason. This season, he is currently averaging 29.8 PPG, 3.5 REB, 6.3 AST, while shooting 51% from the field, 37% from three and 88% from the free-throw line. He's establishing himself as a starting level point guard in the NBA. Jerome will not continue to produce at this level, but he will be a very good fantasy player as long as he is in Memphis. There is still a lot of usage available in Memphis, so it wouldn't be crazy if he averages 23 points per game moving forward. If you're a win-now team, acquiring Jerome might be one of the best bargain plays you can find because of two key reasons. Jerome has two inexpensive years remaining on the three-year, $27.6 million contract he signed last offseason. The Grizzlies could cash in given that he's 29 years old. Jerome has had a lot of injuries during his career which could result in a decline earlier than anticipated. Over the previous three seasons, Jerome played just 87 games, with his lone healthy season coming during his breakout year in Cleveland. There is a world where Jerome remains healthy and ends up being a great point guard into his 30s. There's also a world where he gets hurt again and he ends up not being fast enough to get by defenders, or he just stops hitting his shots at the rate he has been, and he falls out of the league quickly as his body breaks down. With these clear risks, you will not have to pay premium value in dynasty leagues for the production he's giving you. Leonard Miller, Chicago Bulls Miller has found favor in the eyes of new coach Tiago Splitter where he is getting a full-time consistent role for the first time in his career. Last season for Chicago, Miller averaged 11.7 PPG, 5.8 REB, shooting 55.5% FG/35.6% 3PT/76.2% FT on 23.1 minutes. On a per-36 minute basis, he averaged 18 points and nine rebounds. Tiago has had some success with Deni Avdija , and Leonard is a similar player in terms of his game as a driver. The 22-year-old (23 next month) is unlikely to overtake Matas Buzelis or Caleb Wilson in the rotation, but his scoring and rebounding could make him a valuable option in deeper fantasy leagues. He also has the potential to deliver top-100 value if given a starting role. Leonard Miller is ready for a career year 19 points | 7-11 FG | 2-5 from three pic.twitter.com/n2SsRKXVlb — Chicago Bulls (@chicagobulls) October 23, 2026 Dynasty Fallers of the Week Kristaps Porziņģis, Golden State Warriors The biggest faller of the week is undoubtedly Kristaps Porziņģis , who is reportedly "contemplating his future in basketball" with recurring symptoms of POTS (postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome), per Shams Charania of ESPN . For those unfamiliar, POTS is a disorder of the autonomic nervous system , which regulates functions such as heart rate and blood pressure. The condition can cause an excessive increase in heart rate when standing, along with symptoms such as dizziness, fatigue and difficulty tolerating exercise. At the end of the day, medical retirement is absolutely in the realm of possibilities. Naturally, that will hamper any return you’ll get if he’s on your roster in a dynasty league. Porziņģis has a $20 million player option for next season, but only $3 million is guaranteed. If you're a rebuilding dynasty manager with Porziņģis, you have to sell him for whatever you can get. If you're a contending team, I would be interested in giving up any of the following for him. A 2027 second-round pick that is outside the top 35 to get him given how this upcoming second round is going to look. A top 300 dynasty asset on the chance that Porziņģis gives it one more go. The hope is that you get top 150 production for a month or two in your playoffs. It's a pure risk and it might end up not working out, but if you're trying to win, you should be trying to take that risk if the price is low enough. Maybe it's someone like Cody Williams or Kentavious Caldwell-Pope if your league is that deep. Jalen Williams, Oklahoma City Thunder On October 25, Jalen Williams went down with a gruesome injury which resulted in a dislocated left ankle and fractured fibula. He is expected to miss significant time and potentially the rest of the season. Comparable injuries in recent NBA history include those suffered by Paul George and Gordon Hayward . George eventually returned to form whereas Hayward was never the same after the injury, although he remained productive. We will need to knock Williams down dynasty rankings but do not panic sell him. He is still a top-40 dynasty asset at worst and likely belongs closer to the top 30. There will be managers trying to buy low and hoping you accept a deal that is way lower than it should be. Do not do it. If I'm selling Jalen, I would want someone on a similar timeline that's also an established fantasy star. An example of this would be Franz Wagner , Deni Avdija , Paolo Banchero , or Jalen Duren . I also would be fine holding until he gets back and then reassessing the situation. Prospect Corner The college basketball season is right around the corner. Let’s take a look at some of the most intriguing matchups involving NBA Draft prospects. As a dynasty manager, it will be important to keep tabs on these prospects as they could be the future for your team. Here's a look ahead to next Monday when the college season starts with two big prospect matchups. Ohio State vs. BYU (9 ET) Anthony Thompson (Ohio State) and Bruce Branch (BYU) are projected top 10 picks on most mainstream mocks. Both are wings who are projected to be in the 3-and-D role. UCLA vs. Arizona (10 ET) Nikola Kusturica is a projected top-three pick in the 2028 NBA Draft, and Arizona has 3 potential lottery picks with Caleb Holt , Motiejus Krivas , and Ivan Kharchenkov .

stories.title: What is wrong with the Phoenix Suns?
stories.summary: The Phoenix Suns have not looked promising through their first 3 games.
stories.detailText: OKLAHOMA CITY, OKLAHOMA - OCTOBER 26: Devin Booker #15 of the Phoenix Suns handles the ball while being defended by Kenrich Williams and Jared McCain #3 of the Oklahoma City Thunder during the first half at Paycom Center on October 26, 2026 in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Joshua Gateley/Getty Images) | Getty Images Three points. One make on seven shots. Two nights after breaking a franchise record with 43 against Golden State, Devin Booker posted his lowest-scoring night since his rookie season, and the Phoenix Suns got pushed around in Oklahoma City. It wasn’t just Devin Booker’s fault. Or Miles Bridges’ fault. Or Dillon Brooks. Or Jordan Ott. It was everyone, collectively. You could pinpoint so many different issues happening simultaneously… it’s not encouraging. The most frustrating part? This was the softest the Thunder will look all year. They were on the second night of a back-to-back, missing Jalen Williams after a brutal injury, and they lost Alex Caruso in the second quarter. No Chet, no Cason Wallace. It didn’t matter. OKC still controlled the game wire to wire. And yes, even with the injuries, they are still a very good team. I am not saying the Suns had to win, but I expected a little more competitiveness in this one. Three games in, nobody should be writing off this season. But the loss put a spotlight on problems that have been building since opening night: a hit-or-miss franchise player, a team constantly losing the rebounding fight, and an offense with no clear identity. And it wasn’t just this loss, or the 41-point loss on Opening Night, that made me feel uneasy about this team. Even their win against the Warriors’ backup squad looked sloppy. Should Booker force the issue? After his 43-point, 7-rebound, 7-assist opener, Booker said he wanted to be more assertive this season. In OKC, he took seven shots. Give the Thunder credit for the game plan, but Booker owns a big piece of this one. When your franchise player goes passive, the whole roster feels it. Suns fans would rather see Booker go 2-for-15 hunting his shot than 1-for-7 waiting for the game to come to him. Nobody blinks at a superstar forcing it to get going. The playmaking dried up too, and his frustration showed on several possessions. I’m not suggesting he shoots over three defenders as he mentioned postgame, but there were times I thought he played a bit too passively. "I've got to look at it back. Shoot over three people?" Devin Booker after 3-point effort (1-of-7 FG) in Suns loss tonight at OKC after scoring 43 points in Saturday's win over Golden State. "I don't know. We'll see. Like I said, be more creative and finding spots where I get… pic.twitter.com/iGzex8x4wM — Duane Rankin (@DuaneRankin) October 27, 2026 There’s a bigger issue underneath. Teams can load up on Booker this easily because the unit around him doesn’t punish them for it. That’s a roster construction problem that has been sitting there all along, and the Thunder exploited it. So, What’s the Issue? The talent is there. The starters just haven’t figured out how to play together yet. Possessions stall, the ball sticks, and too many trips end in a contested jumper. The Suns play too small and do not gang rebound to make up for their deficiencies on that end. The question is… is the fit there? I think not. Does that mean it won’t change? Absolutely not, but there need to be significant structural adjustments made for this to work. The Brooks and Bridges pairing sums it up: roughly 5-of-20 combined from three, minimal playmaking, and very little ball movement between them. It makes for a disjointed watch, and it puts even more weight on Booker to create everything. What stings most is the offseason message. Continuity was the selling point all summer, with the whole group in the gym together and a reputation as one of the hardest-working rosters in years. You’d expect that team to come out of the gate faster than this. View Link There have been bright spots. Jalen Green looked comfortable early and finished with 20 points, 4 rebounds, and 4 assists on 8-of-13 shooting, and he and Maluach connected on a sharp backdoor feed for an easy finish. Luke Kennard, Goodwin, and Collin Gillespie combined to go 10-of-21 from deep. I will try my best to pump the brakes on the panic, but not ignore the film. It’s a fine line. Last season’s group started 1-4 and still found its way to 45 wins. This roster can turn it around too, as long as players accept some sacrifices and some new roles. If not? It could get ugly.

stories.title: Is Jarred Vanderbilt a solution at backup center for the Lakers?
stories.summary: The Lakers need a solution at backup center. Could Jarred Vanderbilt fill that void?
stories.detailText: SACRAMENTO, CA - OCTOBER 5: Jarred Vanderbilt #2 of the Los Angeles Lakers drives to the basket during the game against the Sacramento Kings during a 2026 NBA Preseason game on October 5, 2026 at Golden 1 Center in Sacramento, California. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Rocky Widner/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images The Lakers’ unbeaten start has been exciting, but there are still worrying signs that have emerged, perhaps none more so than the team’s lack of depth at center. Kevon Looney has struggled in the opening three games of the season and hasn’t played in the second half of the last two contests. Naturally, that was a big talking point in this week’s mailbag , which included solutions for the problem either externally or internally. Let’s dive in! Does JJ think that Vando started the Pallisades Fires? Should be blink twice if Reddick has stolen his dog, too? Does Vando need someone to free him from JJ like Charles and Jake got Jay Chandrasekhar away from Nutraboom? Can we really spend a whole season with Vando and Hardy taking nearly $20 million of salary cap space like we had done with Kleber last year? — Johnny Tuttle It’s pretty clear Kevon Looney is not going to be playable in most matchups this season and the Lakers are going to need a viable backup center. It’s rare for trades to be made before Dec. 15, though not impossible. Still, the Lakers will likely have to look internally for the opening months of the season before most teams are willing to discuss deals. So far, the solution has been playing Sandro Mamukelashvili at center. But there’s also been a growing call for Jarred Vanderbilt, who has been buried on the bench since the start of the preseason. On the one hand, this is different from his usual situation. He’s not needed as a wing this time around. In theory, that means his weakness as a 3-point shooter wouldn’t be as glaring while his strengths as a rebounder could flourish. If the team is going to have five-out spacing without a traditional center, it means Vando won’t clog as much up offensively. On the other hand, Vando’s shortcomings on that end of the floor are often summed up as an inability to hit threes. However, he also can’t finish around the rim, either. From a scoring standpoint, he’s a black hole offensively and hasn’t made any sort of gains on that end. That remains the biggest issue for him getting playing time. Defenses are just never going to respect him offensively, which throws off the spacing on that end of the floor and negates the five-out offense they’re trying to run. As things stand, things are working with Mamu at center and the Lakers don’t particularly need Vando to play. There is an argument for him to get a shot, and maybe it plays out a bit differently this time given the circumstances, but it’s also easy to see how the same problems causing many of the same issues again. Everyone’s asking about finding a backup big. What options are available overseas, and more importantly, how does it work if the Lakeshow were to identify a player they wanted to sign (already knowing that they’d have to trade someone or release another player)? Is there a waiting period? If a buyout is required, is it counted against the cap? — Coops Knee Highs It’s pretty unlikely the Lakers will sign a player overseas midseason, but it isn’t impossible. Most any player who signs in Europe who has any chance of playing in the NBA has a buyout in their contract. That buyout doesn’t count against the cap. Having said all that, it’s unlikely the Lakers are going that route to address the issue for a number of reasons. If a player is going to Europe at this stage in their career, it’s almost always because the NBA interest is gone. There’s a reason you rarely hear about a player coming over from Europe or Asia in January and making an impact on an NBA team. The bigs we’re talking about playing overseas who were recently in the NBA are players like Kelly Olynyk and Maxi Kleber. With all due respect as a blogger sitting in his home office, the drop in talent is quite large. Kendrick Nunn flamed out badly with the Lakers and is thriving in Europe as one of the best players . Talen Horton-Tucker is a borderline top-10 player. There’s a career to be had for a certain level of player and I actually would encourage more players to make that jump to Europe. But it’s not a place teams find in-season upgrades. With centers on contending teams like Jalen Duren and Joel Embiid already missing games, how urgent is the need to find and trade for another center behind Kessler and have the Lakers shown themselves to be enough of a contender that they should be be willing to overpay to beat teams like Philly and Detroit, who may have more tradable assets to work with, to the punch in order to acquire one before the market becomes even more limited? An alternative phrasing might be, how viable is Mamu as a smallball, floor stretching, backup center instead of Looney? — SirTuppy A backup center is so far the only glaring need through 3 games. I feel like there’s one more move they’ll need to establish themselves as true contenders, but what move is it exactly? Who are the potential targets for either move? — nesto2k While I do think the Lakers need a backup center, it’s still too early to tell how urgent that need is. Through the opening three games, Mamu has been sufficient more often than not as a spacing five and the team is going to figure out ways to maximize those lineups as things go. I also wouldn’t be surprised if the team is looking at potential two-way big men to potentially step in and get some spot minutes. That’s a lot easier path to find players and the team has had success with two-way signings in recent years. As things stand, I don’t think there’s a race to get a backup big man, even with recent injuries. Neither Jalen Duren nor Joel Embiid is out long-term, though the Sixers are likely also searching for a backup big man after Ariel Hukporti’s injury. We’ll see how things shake out in the coming weeks and months with rotations and playing time, but a couple names worth monitoring are Jericho Sims, who is not in the rotation for Milwaukee despite them wanting two second round picks for him, and Karlo Matkovic, who was linked to the Lakers previously and is on the edge of the rotation in New Orleans. MIAMI, FL – OCTOBER 8: Karlo Matkovic #17 of the New Orleans Pelicans handles the ball during the game against the Miami Heat on October 8, 2026 at Kaseya Center in Miami, Florida. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this Photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photo by Issac Baldizon/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images I haven’t seen anything offensively from Kessler other than lobs. He’s been awesome, but does he have any sort of post-up game or offensive moves? Is that something that you foresee the Lakers using or is he just a lob threat? — KershawsLegacy I wouldn’t hold my breath on getting a look at the post moves of Kessler. The asks of him offensively will be very streamlined in that he needs to roll to the rim and dunk. That’s obviously oversimplified, but they aren’t tossing him the ball on the left block and having him create a look for himself late in the clock. I do expect there to be growth with him in the short roll, which might lead to him showing off a bit of a floater or intermediate game. Sexton has been off the ball quite a bit so far, even though he’s most effective with the ball in his hands. Is this a Redick issue, or is this a (foreseeable) fit issue playing next to two usage-heavy star creators? — Raison dBasketball Sexton has played two basketball games alongside Luka Dončić and Austin Reaves, so I struggle to have too many takeaways from how he’s used yet. I don’t imagine the team brought him in to be a guard just standing around the perimeter watching Luka or Austin work. At the same time, Luka and Austin are going to have the ball a lot. The opening weeks and months of the season will be the team finding the right balance between optimizing him while also keeping the ball in the hands of your best players. stories.title: Inside the stunning 72-hour Lakers sale -- and the uncertainty that still looms
stories.summary: Three days of secret talks resulted in Mark Walter flipping the Lakers -- and reignited yet another round of bickering among the six Buss siblings.
stories.detailText: BOB IGER WAS on his 213-foot sailing superyacht on Aug. 12, winding down a monthlong vacation in Europe following a historic, two-decade run as CEO of Disney. The biggest event of the day was supposed to be the first total solar eclipse over the continent in more than a century. Millions of tourists, including Iger, had booked vacations along the eclipse's path from Greenland to Southern Spain during the syzygy -- a word derived from Ancient Greek for "yoked together" -- which describes a rare astronomical event in which three or more celestial bodies align in a straight line. During a solar eclipse, the moon sits exactly between the sun and Earth, casting its shadow onto Earth. Some enjoy the rare view -- through special sunglasses. Others ascribe great meaning and magic to eclipses. As those tourists headed to viewing spots for the solar eclipse across Europe, Iger was in a wholly different syzygy with his longtime friend and business partner Josh Kushner and Los Angeles Lakers owner Mark Walter. The alignment of three financial heavy hitters was about to turn what should have been a once-in-a-generation event -- last year's record-breaking sale of the Lakers from the Buss family to Walter -- into the NBA's most shocking news -- again. Instead of getting into position to watch the solar eclipse, Iger was furiously working the phones from Italy to consummate a stunning event of his own -- a $12.5 billion sale of the Lakers seemingly out of nowhere, creating an eclipse unto itself across the worlds of sports and business. Little did anyone know that these secret, cross-continental talks were about to put the Lakers in significant transition yet again -- with new owners evaluating everything and everyone; squabbling former owners again jostling for power and money; and an overhauled roster finally built in the image of its superstar, Luka Doncic . Interviews with more than a dozen team insiders, league executives and others with intimate knowledge of the sale reveal how the deal, which was made over a furious 72 hours, upstaged an already-transformative offseason -- and reignited yet another unresolved round of messy public bickering among the six Buss siblings that still hangs uncomfortably over the beginning of this new season. JUST A YEAR ago, Lakers governor Jeanie Buss had shocked the sports world by negotiating a sale to Walter after 46 years of family ownership. Though that deal was eventually approved by all six siblings, it was not a clean process. According to several family sources, younger brothers Joey and Jesse Buss -- who, because of a "last-man standing" provision in Dr. Jerry Buss's family trust, were positioned to run the team one day after their older siblings died -- hadn't responded to the vote when the sale was initially announced. If the family was going to sell, Joey and Jesse wanted to be a part of the process. They had recently pitched to the other siblings a way to sell a minority share -- albeit, sources with knowledge of the discussions said, at a lower valuation than the $10 billion their older sister subsequently agreed to in the deal with Walter. The younger Buss brothers eventually joined their four older siblings in voting for the sale to Walter, but the process created animosity. Several siblings grumbled that Jeanie had not opened the bidding to outside buyers and had, instead, negotiated directly with Walter, multiple family sources said. Walter, who already owned 27% of the Lakers, had the right of first refusal on any eventual sale of the Buss family's remaining shares, but how did anyone know how much the team would've fetched without actually putting it on the open market? The relationship between Jeanie and her siblings disintegrated further when the Lakers, with Jeanie's approval, fired Janie, Joey and Jesse from their respective positions with the franchise within two months of closing on the sale. All three had expected they'd keep their roles for at least some time while Jeanie was still the controlling owner, multiple family sources said. The deal with Walter included contractual language to keep Jeanie in charge for the next five seasons but contained no such protections for any other family members. Janie told ESPN's Baxter Holmes last season that her sister's actions had made her feel disrespected, like a "crumpled-up piece of paper thrown into the trash." She cited the desires of their father, who had purchased the Lakers in 1979 and died in 2013. "I don't think my dad would be happy with the way things just went down," Janie told Holmes. "Not at all." There was even more consternation, those sources said, when the Buss family members were suddenly charged more for hospitality and their tickets to Lakers games shortly before the start of the playoffs as part of a larger restructuring of Lakers business practices. That familial tension simmered throughout last season -- and came to a boil once again this summer. FOR MUCH OF 2026, Iger and Kushner had been leading a group bidding for the potential Las Vegas NBA expansion franchise, which the NBA initially projected to go for $6 billion-$8 billion, according to industry and ownership sources. But those bids had blown by that threshold, those sources said, and were approaching the then-record $10 billion valuation of Walter's sale. Whichever group won the expansion bid would likely then need to spend what multiple sources estimated would be an additional $2 billion -- at least -- to build an arena in Las Vegas. The Kushner-Iger group had been regarded as one of the favorites to land the team. Iger has had a longtime business relationship with NBA commissioner Adam Silver, from Iger's days negotiating broadcast rights deals for ABC/ESPN with the NBA. In 2020, the two collaborated with the NBPA to create "the bubble" at the Walt Disney Resorts in Orlando, Florida, where the NBA finished its season amid the COVID-19 pandemic. Iger had also been a longtime season-ticket holder of the LA Clippers , although he notably canceled them last season over the team's treatment of Chris Paul, a close friend of Iger's, sources close to him said. Other finalists for the Las Vegas expansion franchise included groups headed by Walmart heiress Nancy Walton Laurie and her husband Bill Laurie; Las Vegas Golden Knights owner Bill Foley and former Phoenix Suns CEO Jerry Colangelo; and Canadian businessman Steve Apostolopoulos and former Milwaukee Bucks owner Marc Lasry. As the Aug. 10 deadline for bids approached, Kushner and Iger discussed their options. Over the past two decades, the 41-year-old Kushner had made a fortune building his venture capital fund, Thrive Capital, with investments in technology companies such as Instagram, Spotify, Twitch, Stripe and OpenAI. This year, Kushner started a new fund, Thrive Eternal, as a hedge against artificial intelligence. "These are assets with qualities that cannot be replicated by technology," Thrive Eternal says on its website. "Iconic franchises and cultural institutions rooted in tradition, identity, and shared experience. In a world shaped by abundant intelligence where creation scales and distribution fragments, we believe they will matter even more." An expansion team is not exactly an iconic brand or a legacy franchise. The Lakers, New York Knicks , Chicago Bulls and Boston Celtics are. None of those was known to be for sale, however. The Knicks had just won an NBA title. The Celtics and Lakers had recently been sold to new owners for record amounts. The Bulls were firmly in the hands of the Reinsdorf family, who have not shown any interest in selling. Still, Kushner and Iger kicked around the idea. Would any of the owners of those franchises take a phone call or listen to an offer? How much would it take to pique their interest? It was a bold, risky pivot to even make calls while they were in the throes of the expansion process. If word got out that they were considering moving away from the expansion franchise, would it risk their standing with the NBA? Whatever they did would need to be quick -- and quiet. WALTER WAS ON a ranch with spotty cellphone service on Aug. 9, when he got a call from a friend, asking whether he'd consider selling the Lakers, according to three sources with knowledge of his whereabouts and thinking. The first conversation was short. The Lakers weren't for sale, Walter told his friend, who relayed the message to Kushner and Iger. But the two businessmen had reason to persevere in their efforts. Two days earlier, on Aug. 7, they had called a well-connected financial industry source who was close enough to Walter to suggest he might be looking to restructure some of his business assets amid federal investigations of alleged fraud within his sprawling $365 billion financial empire, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the conversations. They figured it was worth dropping a line in the water, baiting the hook at a number that would make him think about it. The only catch was they needed an answer within 24 hours. There was no time for a long negotiation or intermediaries. Kushner made the next call to Walter, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the negotiation, and Kushner offered to buy Walter's shares at a $12.5 billion valuation -- a 25% increase in 14 months. It was the kind of staggering "Godfather offer" Walter had presented to Jeanie Buss when he convinced her to sell him the majority of her family's shares a year earlier. Walter decided to cut short his weekend trip and get to a place with better cellphone reception. They had his attention. By Monday, he had returned to his estate in White Oak, Florida. He called his wife, Kimbra, and daughter, Samantha, and asked what they thought of him selling the Lakers. He outlined the enormous return he'd make at this valuation -- nearly $4 billion because he had bought the first 27% of his Lakers shares at a $5 billion valuation in 2021 -- and the benefits that liquidity could provide him, given the remediation plans he had proposed to state insurance regulators. Neither his wife nor daughter had an issue with him selling the Lakers, those sources said. They had been involved with the Los Angeles Dodgers for 14 years, but their attachment to the Lakers was still new. After Walter's family signed off, the circle of people involved in the negotiations widened. Advisers on both sides were sworn to secrecy. There wasn't time for Kushner and Iger's group to do anything resembling due diligence. They were buying the brand, as is, with as quick a close as you'll ever see in a $12.5 billion deal. By the evening of Aug. 11 -- 72 hours after the idea had first been presented to him -- Walter had come to an agreement with Iger and Kushner. JEANIE BUSS LEARNED of Walter's agreement to sell his shares of the Lakers hours before ESPN reported the news on the morning of Aug. 12, according to multiple sources with knowledge of their conversations. She was stunned, according to sources close to her. This was not what she had planned for or expected when she reached out to Walter in 2021 to suggest he purchase Philip Anschutz's shares to become the largest minority shareholder in the franchise, and with it, hold the first right of refusal to buy the Buss family's shares for a controlling interest in the team. Walter and Buss had built a relationship over many years before he expressed an interest in buying into the Lakers. Over the decade he owned the Dodgers, Walter had actively built bridges between L.A.'s premier baseball team and its basketball team. Lakers legend Magic Johnson was part of Walter's ownership group. Dodgers players were often invited to and hosted at Lakers games, and vice versa. Walter often attended games with Buss, while Buss attended Dodgers games with Walter. At the time he bought Anschutz's shares, only people very close to the situation understood why it was so significant. Buss had essentially chosen Walter as her successor. Whenever she was ready to sell her family's controlling shares, he would have the inside track to buy them. Buss chose Walter, multiple sources close to her said, because of how he owned and operated the Dodgers and the positive reviews he had gotten from associates of hers, including Johnson, tennis legend Billie Jean King and longtime Dodgers executive Lon Rosen. She had compared him to her father, Dr. Jerry Buss, for his commitment to winning publicly and privately over the years. To those close to the situation, the question wasn't whether the Buss family would eventually sell to Walter but when. Older brothers Johnny and Jim had wanted to sell the team for years. Jeanie, her sister Janie and younger brothers Joey and Jesse still had roles with the team and wanted to stay on longer. In 2025, Walter came up with an offer he thought would make everyone happy: a $10 billion valuation -- generating approximately $800 million for each sibling -- and an agreement for Jeanie to stay on as controlling owner for five years, codified in writing as part of the agreement. "Over the past decade, I have come to know Mark well -- first as a businessman, then as a friend and now as a colleague," Jeanie Buss said in a statement after the sale. "He has demonstrated time and time again his commitment to bringing championships to Los Angeles, and, on behalf of Lakers fans everywhere, I am beyond excited about what our future has in store." Buss even showed that paperwork to Doncic and his team, his manager Lara Beth Seager said, to reassure them that she would still have final say over his basketball future. Doncic had learned the hard way how an ownership change could affect him after his shocking trade from the Dallas Mavericks to the Lakers in February 2025. Former Mavericks owner Mark Cuban also thought he'd be allowed to stay on as head of basketball operations when he sold his controlling stake to the Adelson family in 2023. Cuban swore to Doncic that he wanted him to be a Maverick for life, but wasn't involved or included in the trade discussions that sent Doncic to L.A. This time, it was Jeanie who would learn the hard way -- that whatever relationship she had built with Walter and others would be superseded by the harsh realities of the modern business world. DESPITE THAT RELATIONSHIP, the man Jeanie chose as the next steward of the Lakers was not the rock-solid titan of the financial industry he appeared to be. Walter, the public would soon learn, was under multiple federal criminal investigations before his purchase of the Lakers became official at the end of October. According to the Wall Street Journal, the FBI on Sept. 18, 2025, conducted a raid of a private plane at Chicago's Midway Airport, where Walter had been traveling, and seized a laptop and mobile phone. Just 10 months later, Walter flipped the Lakers like a cold asset, not a crown-jewel, generational investment. After five decades of family ownership, Jeanie had relinquished control of her family's most prized possession to someone who had treated it no differently than any other line item in his massive portfolio. "I mean, he made $2.5 billion in 10 months by flipping the Lakers like a spec house," one family confidant said. "But that wasn't supposed to be the deal. Jeanie picked him because he was going to own it like he's owned the Dodgers." Walter has not spoken publicly about the sale outside of an initial statement he released to ESPN. In late August, his company, The Walter Group, issued a statement asserting it had been subjected to "multipronged attacks" from "unnamed sources with self-serving interests." The statement said that TWG and its Group 1001 insurance companies had presented a plan to state insurance regulators to address regulatory concerns over a percentage of affiliated transactions it had misreported in its filings. TWG explained that the affiliated transactions in question are "common across the insurance industry" and "suggestions that TWG is looting insurers is defamatory and false." Investigators are still looking into the company's dealings as it makes changes in the way it operates. TWG Global announced in late August that it had swapped out $6.5 billion of its assets to replace the type of affiliated loans regulators had taken issue with. The dual sales of the Lakers and Walter's minority 12.8% stake in Premier League club Chelsea have raised additional capital, while also leading to an assortment of buyers inquiring about the availability of the Dodgers and Los Angeles Sparks. The company has emphatically denied that it is looking to sell its sports assets at "fire sale" prices to raise capital for its insurance operations. The sales of the Lakers and Chelsea came in at significant valuations -- a record in the case of the Lakers. However, sources with knowledge of the situation confirm a Bloomberg report that acknowledged there have been early-stage discussions about the Sparks at what would be a similarly massive valuation, estimated at $700 million. Inquiries for the Dodgers have thus far been rebuffed, those sources said. IGER LANDED BACK home in Los Angeles a few days after the sale agreement was reached. The first visitor he entertained at his house was Jeanie Buss, according to multiple sources with knowledge of the meeting. He had given public comments to the California Post immediately after news of the sale broke that the new ownership group intended to honor the agreement Buss had with Walter to stay on as controlling owner, but added, "if something changes, then it changes." Despite the public hedge, Iger reaffirmed his commitment to Jeanie to maintain a role after the sale closes when they met, those sources said. They have stayed in regular contact since then. Whether she'll be able to do so -- and what that role ultimately is -- depends on how the latest round of family discord is resolved. By the time Walter decided to sell his stake in the Lakers in mid-August, family sources said there had already been renewed calls among the siblings to sell the remaining 17.8% of the team that the family owned. The Lakers had fired four of her siblings already. Jim Buss, who was fired in 2017, noted to the group that there was little justification for keeping the family's remaining shares, other than nostalgia and Jeanie keeping her controlling-ownership power for four additional years, according to multiple family sources. He circulated a proposal he hoped would satisfy all parties. On the night of Aug. 10, two days before the sale, Lakers vice president of finance Joe McCormack called for a meeting of the Buss siblings to discuss a dissolution of the family trust and seek approval to lock down all family shares for four years under a new trust, according to ESPN's Dave McMenamin. When the family discussed McCormack's proposal on Aug. 11, no mention was made of Walter's impending sale to Kushner and Iger. The family woke up to the news of the massive sale the following morning like everyone else. On Aug. 17, ESPN's Shams Charania reported that Johnny, Jim, Janie, Joey and Jesse Buss had voted to sell the remaining family shares to Iger and Kushner, using "go-along" rights they had been given as part of the sale to Walter. (Technically, those rights can be only invoked once Walter officially notifies the family that he has signed a deal to sell, which hasn't happened yet.) Jeanie was the only family member who did not vote to sell. In fact, she did not even respond to the vote that had been called a week earlier. Later that day, her lawyer, Adam Streisand, sent a letter to the five siblings, challenging the legality of their vote based on a 2017 court order that required the two co-trustees, Janie and Joey, to always vote to ensure she remained the controlling owner of the team. The siblings immediately responded to Streisand's initial letter with a statement of their own, reaffirming their desire to sell. They contended they needed only a majority (four of six votes and two of three co-trustees) to enact that go-along provision, according to sources with knowledge of the siblings' position. Jeanie currently controls the Buss family trust, which owns 17.8% of the Lakers. NBA rules mandate that a controlling owner must own at least 15% of the team. An alternate governor must own at least 5%. Still, multiple family sources said there have been settlement talks between the two sides over the past two months. Each sibling stands to make an additional $371 million if the family sells the entirety of its shares via the go-along provision. The siblings could also try to find a buyer at a higher valuation, a possibility fueled by a pitch, which The Wall Street Journal obtained, to Thrive Eternal investors in which the company projected the Lakers valuation to be at least $30 billion within a decade. The dispute spilled back into the public on Oct. 7, when the five siblings formally filed a response to Jeanie's suit. "Jimmy, Johnny, Janie, Joey and Jesse Buss, the five of six siblings who voted to sell the Trust's shares in the Lakers, today filed their formal opposition, demonstrating that Jeanie Buss's petition is legally and factually baseless," the siblings said in a statement issued to ESPN. "While discussions among the siblings continue, their focus remains on facilitating the proposed transaction and the [Buss family] trust's participation in it, while ensuring that all beneficiaries, including Jeanie, are treated equally." Nine days later, the five siblings submitted, on behalf of Joey and Janie, an additional filing, this one challenging Jeanie and her previous petition that seeks to remove them as co-trustees and void the siblings' 5-1 vote to sell the family's remaining stake in the team. Through it all, the foundation of the dispute remains the same: whether the five siblings can sell their share of the team without Jeanie's approval. A court date is set for Dec. 8 if no settlement is reached. DONCIC WAS THE only person outside of the small circle of people close to Walter, Kushner and Iger who had any inkling how the sports world was about to dramatically change before Aug. 12. The last time he had gotten a text from Seager, his longtime manager, at an odd hour was in February 2025, when she reached him after midnight and told him he had been traded to the Lakers. This time, she had gotten a tip well after midnight at her home in Dallas that something big might be happening again. She texted Doncic, who was just waking up in Slovenia, alerting him to the possibility. All summer, they had been planning a five-day team bonding retreat in Doncic's home country for his new Lakers teammates. On the first night, they'd all eat at his favorite restaurant, Cubo, in his hometown of Ljubljana. Then, they'd play golf some 40 miles north on the perfectly manicured grounds of Royal Bled, sitting in a valley beneath the tree-lined peaks of the Alps. Another day was built around rowing lessons on Lake Bled, taught by Slovenian Olympian Jani Klemencic. Three high-speed boats, 15 Lakers, learning to row together. Then, in one early-morning text, all those plans seemed secondary. It was a stunning turn with no forewarning. Just a week earlier, Seager had met Jeanie and Rosen for dinner. Nothing had seemed amiss. At that point, Kushner had yet to engage Walter about the possibility of buying the Lakers. Doncic had developed a good relationship with Walter and Jeanie Buss in the 18 months since he had come to Los Angeles, meeting and texting with both of them regularly. Walter even took him and a group of teammates to a Backstreet Boys concert at The Sphere in Las Vegas last summer, after Doncic agreed to a three-year, $165 million contract extension with the Lakers. If the sale goes through and Kushner and Iger are approved by the NBA, and that is expected to happen by the end of the year or early next year, according to multiple sources close to the sale process, they'd be his fifth team owners across two franchises in the past three years. By the time Seager called Doncic to tell him the deal was done, he had already processed the initial shock. "There's not much that can shock me anymore," Doncic told her. The next day, as he congratulated the new owners, he acknowledged the seismic move and posted on X: "I've gotten used to big changes over these last few years."

stories.summary: Jayson Tatum, Paul George, and Mitchell Robinson are all not on the injury report despite Tuesday’s Celtics game being on the second night of a back-to-back.
