stories.title: BREAKING: Colts trade DeForest Buckner back to San Francisco 49ers for fourth-round pick
stories.summary: The Colts continue its roster overhaul, sending its veteran defensive tackle back to the team that drafted him in 2016.
stories.detailText: INDIANAPOLIS, IN - SEPTEMBER 27: Indianapolis Colts defensive tackle DeForest Buckner (99) reacts after the NFL game between the Houston Texans and the Indianapolis Colts on September 27, 2026, at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Michael Allio/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Indianapolis Colts are continuing their roster overhaul, trading three-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle DeForest Buckner to the San Francisco 49ers in exchange for a 2027 fourth-round pick, according to NFL insider Tom Pelissero. The move comes just hours after Indianapolis traded eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks for a 2027 third-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round selection. With the Colts sitting at 2-5 and having lost three consecutive games, the organization appears to be fully embracing its role as a seller ahead of the November 10 trade deadline. For Buckner, the trade represents a reunion with the organization that originally selected him seventh overall in the 2016 NFL Draft. He spent his first four seasons in San Francisco, developing into one of the league’s premier interior defensive linemen and helping the 49ers reach Super Bowl LIV following the 2019 season. Indianapolis acquired Buckner in March 2020 in exchange for the 13th overall pick in that year’s draft, immediately signing him to a four-year, $84 million extension. The move was one of the most significant acquisitions of former general manager Chris Ballard’s tenure and provided the Colts with an established defensive star who would become the centerpiece of their defensive line for more than six seasons. Buckner certainly lived up to expectations individually. He earned First-Team All-Pro honors during his first season in Indianapolis, recording 9.5 sacks and establishing himself as one of the most disruptive interior defenders in football. He followed that performance with several more productive seasons, earning additional Pro Bowl selections in 2021 and 2023 while consistently providing the Colts with a reliable pass-rushing presence. Even at 32 years old, Buckner has shown few signs of slowing down. Through seven games in 2026, he has recorded 31 tackles, four sacks, eight quarterback hits and three passes defended, remaining one of the team’s most productive defensive players despite its struggles throughout the season. However, with Buckner playing out the final year of his contract and Indianapolis potentially entering a rebuilding period, retaining him for the remainder of the season became increasingly difficult to justify. Following the Colts’ embarrassing loss to the previously winless Tennessee Titans, Buckner openly expressed his frustration with the organization’s continued struggles. After more than six seasons in Indianapolis without sustained postseason success, an opportunity to return to San Francisco and compete for a championship could be beneficial for both sides. He showed his frustration again after the Vikings loss. DeForest Buckner on his current level of frustration, via @RomeovilleKid : "I don’t know. How about you guess. Yeah, I’m frustrated. Same thing, we lost." pic.twitter.com/2P3VfPVkaW — Underdog NFL (@UnderdogNFL) October 25, 2026 In my recent evaluation of Buckner’s trade value , I projected that Indianapolis could realistically receive a 2027 fourth-round pick for the veteran defensive tackle, the exact compensation the Colts ultimately acquired. San Francisco was also among the potential destinations identified, given its need for additional defensive line help and Buckner’s previous connection to the organization. Although a fourth-round selection might appear underwhelming for a player of Buckner’s caliber, his age and expiring contract significantly limited his market value. The Colts also faced the possibility of losing him in free agency without receiving any guaranteed compensation, making the opportunity to secure a draft pick in 2027 considerably more appealing. His departure also creates an opportunity for Adetomiwa Adebawore, who has shown encouraging development along Indianapolis’ defensive line. The former fourth-round selection recorded two sacks against Minnesota on Sunday and could receive a significantly larger role over the remainder of the season as the Colts evaluate their younger players. For San Francisco, Buckner provides an established interior pass rusher who could immediately strengthen its defensive front. The 49ers have dealt with injuries throughout their defense, including the loss of Nick Bosa, and bringing back a familiar face with Buckner’s experience and production gives the organization another proven weapon as it pursues a playoff berth. Meanwhile, the Colts have now acquired three additional draft selections through their trades of Nelson and Buckner, including two picks in 2027. With Indianapolis already without its first-round selection next year following the Sauce Gardner trade, replenishing draft capital has become increasingly important for a franchise preparing for significant organizational changes. Buckner’s departure also raises questions about which veterans could be moved next, particularly Jonathan Taylor, Josh Downs and Grover Stewart, whose names have surfaced in trade discussions over the past several days. The Colts have made their intentions increasingly clear. Less than two weeks after firing Ballard, Indianapolis has already parted ways with two of its most accomplished players, and there may be more changes ahead before the deadline.

stories.title: Cowboys run game paves the way in bounce-back win over Eagles
stories.summary: The Cowboys have the ground game working again.
stories.detailText: Photo by Emilee Chinn/Getty Images | Getty Images The Dallas Cowboys needed a win on Monday night in the worst way. Coming off two straight losses and facing off against a Philadelphia Eagles team that was missing key pieces on both sides of the ball, Dallas needed to walk out of Philly with a win to avoid a complete freefall. While they were far from perfect, the Cowboys avoided that third straight loss as their offense led them to a 38-21 win over the beaten-down Eagles. Multiple players on Dallas’ offense had notable performances, but it was their running attack that stole the show, earning them this week’s game ball award. Against the Buccaneers and Packers, the Cowboys couldn’t sustain success in the run game. Dallas totaled 98 rushing yards in the two matchups, and their one-dimensional attack played a role in their losses. On Monday night, for what felt like the first time this season, the Cowboys’ rushing attack set the stage for their offense. Dallas totaled a season-high 204 rushing yards on 38 attempts, averaging 5.4 Y/R as a team. The Cowboys finished with the third-best offensive rush EPA of any team in Week 7 (0.199) while also finishing in the top eight in rush success rate (48.6%). Javonte Williams had a notably impressive performance, recording a career-high 155 rushing yards to go with 82 yards after contact and five missed tackles forced. Williams’ impressive physicality in the run game set the tone for Dallas’ offense from the first snap. Javonte Williams on MNF: 25 carries 155 yards (career high) 1 TD First Cowboy with 150+ rushing yards in a game since Ezekiel Elliott in 2018. pic.twitter.com/xOqz51Kdqq — Underdog NFL (@UnderdogNFL) October 27, 2026 If the Cowboys can continue to have a complementary, balanced attack on the offensive side of the ball like they did on Monday night, they are going to be very hard to slow down.

stories.title: Knockout league pickups: Prioritize running backs while they're available
stories.summary: A confluence of bye weeks and surprisingly poor performances make this the week to bid on a star running back
stories.detailText: If you've been patching together the position in your Knockout league to this point, consider it a prime time to pounce for a top-shelf free agent. Between bye weeks and unexpectedly poor performances, an unusually large number of top-shelf running backs have found themselves on knocked-out teams so far in October. The top 11 running backs in fantasy points per game have found themselves on a knocked-out team in more than 10% of leagues six times in the past three weeks alone. In fact, Derrick Henry , ninth in total points (122.7) and 11th in points per game (17.5), has been on the list in back-to-back weeks, after scoring fewer than 10 points in Weeks 6 (5.0) and 7 (5.9). The last time he had scored in single digits was Week 5 of last season. The bye weeks have had a lot to do with this availability trend. In Week 5, it was RB2 (going by points per game) Kenneth Walker III and RB9 Chuba Hubbard . In Week 6, RB1 Jahmyr Gibbs took his turn. This past week, RB7 James Cook III had his bye. Hubbard was the only one of them whose knocked-out rate finished beneath 10% in that week (he was on eliminated teams in 8.5% of leagues), which you can attribute to the fact that you didn't spend a one of your top two picks on him. It doesn't get any easier on the availability front: RB4 Christian McCaffrey 's bye week is up next, and RB3 Bijan Robinson 's arrives three weeks after that, during Bye-Maggeddon . In a season where having an elite running back has proven particularly advantageous, now is the time to open up your FAB wallet and strengthen the position, assuming, of course, you're not already the lucky manager of one of the aforementioned seven players. Getting one with his bye in the rearview is even more beneficial. This is the first time all season that three of these top 11 positional scorers have found themselves available via free agency in at least 10% of Knockout leagues, and two of them (Cook and Walker) fit the rearview-bye description. Even McCaffrey's managers should consider spending big on a top-shelf running back, bridging the San Francisco 49ers star's bye week, then providing an elite one-two punch for the season's final nine weeks. Remember, piecing together quarterback and wide receiver via the matchups route becomes easier with each passing week as your league size shrinks. There's only so many elite running backs. The 20 most-knocked-out players exiting Week 7 Note that FAB recommendations are in three tiers: "% OF FAB TO BID (ENFORCE)" is a low-end recommendation, if you don't necessarily need the player but don't want him gifted to the competition. "% OF FAB TO BID (MEDIAN)" is the recommended bid for a team with average needs at that position. "% OF FAB TO BID (AGGRESSIVE)" is advised for teams thin at that specific spot. My favorite pickup of the week Kenneth Walker III , RB, Kansas City Chiefs (10.3% Knocked out, 15th overall, RB5): Neither he nor his Chiefs had an especially good Week 7, as he scored a season-low 9.7 fantasy points while his team lost, 20-3. The matchup -- a Sunday Night Football road game against the Seattle Seahawks , who have allowed the fewest yards per game -- had a lot to do with it. Even with that performance, Walker ranks second at his position in total fantasy points (147.7) and fantasy points per game (24.6), as well as second in rushing share (75%) and fifth in snap rate (75%). He's one of the best all-around players to have in any fantasy football format, but he's especially appealing in Knockout play with a rearview bye. Recommended bid: 27-59% of your full-season FAB budget. Go get 'em Josh Allen , QB, Buffalo Bills (11.7% Knocked out, 6th overall, QB1): He's only atop this group and ahead of the next two running backs because he's the top-scoring fantasy quarterback -- and that's not just this year, but also 2020, 2021, 2023 and 2025 -- and he has his bye week in the rearview. I typically prefer to stream my quarterbacks for Knockout play, but Allen is the one for whom you should open up your wallet, given those circumstances. Recommended bid: 20-36%. James Cook III , RB, Buffalo Bills (15.4% Knocked out, 1st overall): He has been a top-eight scoring running back in each of the past three seasons, but if there's anything that keeps him a notch behind the aforementioned Walker, it's what Allen's goal-line presence does to Cook's scoring opportunities. At the goal line so far this year, Allen has handled seven of the team's 11 plays and converted them all; Cook has had three and converted one. Cook is also 5-for-11 converting goal-to-go carries; Allen is 6-for-7. Recommended bid: 24-53%. Derrick Henry , RB, Baltimore Ravens (12.2% Knocked out, 5th overall, RB2): Back-to-back poor weeks might heighten prospective fantasy managers' worries, but Henry's role remains massive and his supporting cast should only improve once Lamar Jackson is fully healthy. Henry leads the league in goal-to-go carries (20), and he's fifth among running backs in rushing share (69%). The only separator between him and Walker or Cook is that Henry's bye week is still ahead of him (Week 13), sandwiched by a pair of brutal matchups (@HOU, BYE, TB from Weeks 12-14). Recommended bid: 22-51%. Bhayshul Tuten , RB, Jacksonville Jaguars (10.6% Knocked out, 12th overall, RB3): He's my stealth rearview-bye running back add, a player you might be able to sneak through at a deep discount bid relative to Walker, Cook or Henry. Tuten isn't quite the primary back that any of those three are -- Chris Rodriguez Jr . does vulture some goal-line carries from him -- but he still has healthy numbers in terms of snap rate (55%) and rushing share (56%). I'm also a believer in the Jaguars' offense, and to make an out-there comp to a 2025 team/running back situation -- much as I'm no fan of such comps -- Tuten is a decent bet to have a Chase Brown -like hot spell to conclude his 2026. Recommended bid: 16-40%. Worthy, with worries Nico Collins , WR, Houston Texans (12.8% Knocked out, 2nd overall, WR1): Well, he's got one worry: His bye, which arrives this very week. Among players (or team defenses) whose knockout rates were greater than league average over the past three weeks, 17% were on bye at the time. Still, if you can steer Collins through his Week 8 absence, he doesn't have a single remaining matchup against one of the 10 toughest schedule-adjusted positional matchups, and he finishes his Knockout season with four straight games against top-12 favorable matchups. Recommended bid: 17-40%. Garrett Wilson , WR, New York Jets (12.6% Knocked out, 4th overall, WR4): Another week, another Wilson inclusion on this list. As his percentage of available remaining weeks declines -- his Week 13 bye becomes decreasingly appealing -- and his percentage of suboptimal matchups increases -- look at that DEN-@ARI-NE-MIN post-bye schedule -- he's going to see his recommended FAB bid plummet. Recommended bid: 12-30% of your full-season FAB budget. No thanks DK Metcalf , WR, Pittsburgh Steelers (10.7% Knocked out, 11th overall, WR6): I'm not impressed by what I've seen from him thus far. He has only two top-25 positional scoring weeks, and has barely averaged 10 fantasy points (10.9, to be exact) despite a 24% target share. Metcalf is third in the league in drops, and his 26% catch rate on throws at least 15 yards downfield is his worst in eight NFL seasons. His bye week also arrives in Week 9, making it just as likely he'll be this available exiting that week as this one. Recommended bid: 7-17%.

stories.title: Behold: Texas executes a mesh concept as poorly as you’ll ever see
stories.summary: This one made Mike Leach roll over in his grave.
stories.detailText: PULLMAN, WASHINGTON - SEPTEMBER 21: Head coach Mike Leach of the Washington State Cougars looks on in the second half against the UCLA Bruins at Martin Stadium on September 21, 2019 in Pullman, Washington. UCLA defeats Washington State 67-63. (Photo by William Mancebo/Getty Images) | Getty Images The mesh concept is an Air Raid staple that remains prevalent across college football, occupying a spot in virtually every playbook, if not every single playbook. For Texas Longhorns head coach Steve Sarkisian, who doesn’t have any Air Raid influences in his background, it’s not a common call, but Sarkisian did dial it up early in the third quarter of Saturday’s win over the Ole Miss Rebels on a 3rd and 3 as the Longhorns tried to find their footing after the sack-fumble. And, let me tell you, this is about as ugly as it gets all around. Hopefully Mike Leach was fishing somewhere in the great beyond and didn’t see it, because otherwise he was rolling over in his grave. Ole Miss blitzes on third and short and Arch Manning is left to throw it to three Texas players in standing in the exact same area of the field. Route tree needs to get cleaned up. This is a first down if Michael Masunas flattens out and opens up to Arch. Hot routes, man. pic.twitter.com/4tV16U1LRC — Tyler Horka (@tbhorka) October 27, 2026 It’s a RB Bunch version with a formation into the boundary that uses freshman wide receiver Jermaine Bishop and fifth-year tight end Michael Masunas as the crossers, one area where this play goes really wrong. The typical teaching point for the crosser is five or six yards of depth and Bishop gets that right, so the larger issue is probably the timing of the play — Masunas uses a stutter release, but Bishop doesn’t. He’s just right into his route trying to beat his man defender, but because he’s so fast, Masunas never has a chance to get the depth he needs. So instead of getting the rub that makes the mesh concept such an enduring man-beater, Bishop and Masunas almost run into each other. The overall spacing on the play just doesn’t work, either, as junior wide receiver Ryan Wingo runs his stop route only two yards deeper than the mesh point because he’s got a defender sitting on his back. The wheel route by fifth-year running back Raleek Brown never has a chance with a defender over the top and another picking Brown up quickly in coverage. Behind center, senior quarterback Arch Manning gets sped up because the left side of the offensive line hasn’t handled an end-tackle twist at all with sophomore left guard Dylan Sikorski and senior left tackle Andre Cojoe getting hung up on the tackle, who does a nice job of splitting them. Fifth-year center Connor Robertson isn’t occupied and should be able to help, but he doesn’t have his eyes right and heads in the other direction. So the timing of the play never really has a chance, causing Manning to lose his footwork and throw the ball to where Bishop might be if he’d been able to actually clear the tight end. The check down is to the field with junior wide receiver Emmet Mosley V in motion, but Manning’s breakdown in footwork doesn’t give him a chance to flip the ball out there, leading to a three and out and a 10-play, 80-yard touchdown drive by Ole Miss and, ultimately, a wasted quarter for the Longhorns. If Manning does get it out to the flat? Mosley is one on one with the safety, who may make the tackle to force a fourth down or may give up a huge play. The play call makes sense — it’s a good call for the down and distance and it works against man and zone coverages, but if Sarkisian wants to keep it on his call sheet, Texas is going to need to rep it more often in practice to actually get the mesh right. Otherwise, it’s just a mess concept.

stories.title: Packers Film Room: Woulda Coulda Shouldas in Week 7
stories.summary: Breaking down a couple plays that could have made a difference in the Packers Week 7 loss to the Lions
stories.detailText: (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s underselling it a bit to say that the Green Bay Packers had a few missed opportunities this past weekend, but there were a couple big ones that stood out that I wanted to spend a bit of time with. I already looked at the field goal operation , so today we’re going to look at a couple of passing plays: the 4th down to Golden in the flat and the incomplete pass to Jacobs just before the blocked field goal. Play 1: 4th & 4, 4:20 remaining in the 2nd quarter Packers are in 11 personnel (1 RB, 1 TE, 3 WR) in a Quad Bunch Nub formation (a 4×1 formation with three receivers in a bunch to one side and the TE in-line on the opposite side of the formation). It’s 11 personnel, but the formation is a bit funky, with Pierre Strong [22] (the RB) the inside man in bunch, and Matthew Golden [0] (a WR) in the backfield. The Packers don’t shift or motion: they walk to the line, Jordan Love [10] gives a quick assessment, then they quick-snap, trying to catch the Lions mid-communication (something they did quite a bit in this game). They’re running a version of Mesh, with Tucker Kraft [85] and Pierre Strong running dueling drag routes, crossing a couple yards down the field. This version is Mesh Sit, with Savion Williams [83] following a drag then pulling up on a Sit route in the middle of the field. Christian Watson [9] is running a corner route and Golden is running a flat route. Typically the read on Mesh would be the vertical route first (Watson on the corner), then the Mesh point (Kraft/Strong, Williams), then the flat if none of those are open (Golden). This version out of Quads is slightly different, in that part of the whole thing is for the bunch receivers to create a wall of commotion for the Flat route. It’s a bit like Mesh Traffic in that regard (we’ll get to that). That would make DJ Reed the most important player on the defense. Love is reading Reed at the snap. With the push from the bunch and the initial angle from Reed, it looks like he’s going to get caught in the wall, which would leave Golden wide open in the flat. Instead, Reed does a really nice job of avoiding contact and maintaining speed over the wall, firing off the hip of Watson and driving down on Golden. Nice rep by Reed. If Reed gets so much as a bump, this is a TD. If Love feels he’s able to wait a tick to throw this, he could see Reed breaking and move off. If that were the case, he could have potentially been able to find Strong on the backside. Unfortunately for Love, Strong would be the 5th read on this play, which would make it tough to work back over to him. There’s a version of this play I like a bit better. A small little change but creates just a bit more traffic to navigate for the defense. This would see Golden align away from the bunch and release through the line (typically through the B gap). We’ve seen the Packers run this a few times over the years. It doesn’t have quite the same pop if it’s a WR in the backfield, but it could still be enough to get the job done. It introduces a few more moving pieces for the offense (slightly longer to set up, hoping the o-line doesn’t get shoved back into the release point, etc.) but it’s a beautiful play. I am certainly not saying that this play absolutely would have worked, but it’s a slightly different take on the same idea. It’s also one of my favorite Mesh variants, so I will bring it up as often as I can. Play 2: 3rd & 5, 3:30 remaining in the 4th quarter Fast forward to the last offensive play of the game for the Packers. Game tied 17-17, facing 3rd & 5. They are – once again – in 11 personnel. Bunch right, RB aligned away from the bunch. The Lions are showing a single-high safety and a lot of bodies around the line. Kraft shifts wide before the snap, leaving a two-man stack of Watson and Golden just outside the right hash. They’re running a little shallow crossing concept between Golden and Kraft, while Watson runs a corner route over the top. On the left side, Josh Jacobs [8] motions out at the snap, giving him outside leverage on his defender. With the initial release of both Savion Williams [83] and Jacobs, it looks like they may be running Arches, a popular concept in this down and distance. Instead, Jacobs gives a little shake and releases vertically up the field, while Williams releases vertically to the inside. On this play, Jacobs would be the Alert (throw this at the top of the drop if given a specific look or simply don’t look at it at all after an initial assessment post-snap). The goal of concept is to work the concept on the right (look to Watson initially, then work to Golden/Kraft underneath) if the Lions rotate back to a two-high safety look after the snap. With the Lions staying in single-high – and Jacobs getting outside leverage on the motion – Love takes the vertical route to Jacobs. The Lions staying in single-high means there are more bodies around the line, making the shorter concept from Golden/Kraft pretty muddy. They had already hit Jacobs on a couple choice routes close to the line earlier in the game, so the defense likely had those in mind. Midway through the 2nd quarter they hit Jacobs on an Angle route on the Texas concept. Then, early in the 3rd, they hit him on an out route (and he scored a TD on it). Derrick Moore [8] is in good coverage down the field, but the hesitation from Jacobs at the assumed break point gives him the initial separation he needs. Love lofts the ball over the top, dropping it in the bucket. I believe Derrick Moore [8] may get a fingertip on this, but it hits Jacobs in both hands and he can’t bring it in. Not too different from the route he ran against the Broncos last year that ended in a TD. Except for the part where he caught the ball. That part was different, I guess. Albums listened to: Chapterhouse – Whirlpool ; Lucy Dacus – Forever is a Feeling ; Teenage Fanclub – Bandwagonesque ; Ethel Cain – Willoughby Tucker, I’ll Always Love You

stories.title: Colts' fire sale continues as Indianapolis trades DT DeForest Buckner back to 49ers
stories.summary: The Indianapolis Colts continued their fire sale, agreeing to trade three-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle DeForest Buckner to the San Francisco 49ers.
stories.detailText: You can go home again − especially if your weekend getaway is in flames. The Indianapolis Colts continued their fire sale on Tuesday, Oct. 27, agreeing to trade three-time Pro Bowl defensive tackle DeForest Buckner to the San Francisco 49ers , his original team. According to multiple reports, the Colts are getting a 2027 fourth-round pick in return for Buckner, who is in the final year of his current contract. Niners tight end George Kittle, a teammate of Buckner's in San Francisco from 2017 through '19 − their final season together concluding with a trip to Super Bowl 54 − celebrated news of the reunion on X. stories.title: 49ers agree to acquire DeForest Buckner from Colts
stories.summary: Buckner is headed back to the team that drafted him at No. 7 overall in 2016.
stories.detailText: DeForest Buckner is headed back to the Bay. The 49ers — who traded Buckner to Indianapolis back in 2020 — have agreed to acquire Buckner from the Colts, according to multiple reports. Indianapolis will receive a 2027 fourth-round pick to complete the deal. While Buckner is in his 11th season, he’s still plenty productive from the interior of the defensive line. He’s recorded 4.0 sacks with four tackles for loss and eight QB hits so far in 2026. He’s also tallied three passes defensed and a fumble recovery. The No. 7 overall pick of the 2016 draft out of Oregon, Buckner was a key piece of San Francisco’s defense in his first four seasons, helping the club advance to Super Bowl LIV to cap the 2019 season. He registered 12.0 sacks for the 49ers in 2018 and 7.5 sacks for the club in 2019. He was traded to the Colts after his fourth season, with Indianapolis signing him to a long-term second contract. In Buckner’s 158 career games, he’s picked up 75.5 sacks, 101 tackles for loss, and 196 QB hits. Buckner has been palpably frustrated by the Colts losses in recent weeks. With an expiring contract, it's no surprise that he's been moved. It's the second high-profile trade of the day from the Colts, who earlier dealt guard Quenton Nelson to the Seahawks.

stories.title: Dave Canales knows opposing offenses are excited to game plan vs. Panthers' run defense
stories.summary: The Panthers have the worst run defense in the NFL, and head coach Dave Canales knows what that means for opposing teams game planning against them.
stories.detailText: The Panthers have the worst run defense in the NFL , and head coach Dave Canales knows what that means for opposing teams game planning against them. Up next for the Panthers is a game on Thursday night against the Packers, who have the most pass-heavy offense in the NFL. Canales said today that after giving up 258 rushing yards on Sunday against the Buccaneers, he knows that the Packers will be excited by the opportunity to play against them. That means both trying to run the ball with Josh Jacobs, and trying to have Jordan Love beat them deep if the Panthers overcompensate for their run defense struggles by stacking the box. "Collectively, as a group, we have to be locked in to what they're going to try to do and how they're going to attack us," Canales said. "I'm sure they're watching the game and they're seeing 250 yards on the ground, and that's got to be appealing. For me, as an offensive-minded coach, I think about that and say, 'We can set some things up down the field by making sure we have a run game going.' That would be my approach, so I do expect them to run the ball, and we do expect Jordan to heave the ball down the field just like he does, and challenge the back half of our defense as well." The Packers, who have only had Jacobs for one game this season, have not run the ball well. Having the Panthers' defense come to town could be just the thing to fix that.

stories.title: Colts reportedly trade DT DeForest Buckner to 49ers
stories.summary: The 32-year-old Buckner is set to become a free agent in the offseason.
stories.detailText: The Indianapolis Colts continued moving players Tuesday, trading defensive tackle DeForest Buckner to the San Francisco 49ers for a 2027 fourth-round draft pick, NFL insider Tom Pelissero reports. Buckner returns to a 49ers team that selected him with the No. 7 pick in the 2016 NFL Draft. A two-time All-Pro and three-time Pro Bowler, Buckner was traded to the Colts in March 2020 after four seasons with the 49ers. In 95 career games in Indianapolis, he recorded 63 total tackles and 47 sacks. Now he's back on a 6-1 49ers team with aspirations to compete for a Super Bowl title this season. He provides an immediate upgrade to a defensive line that's also expecting All-Pro pass rusher Nick Bosa to return soon. General manager John Lynch told reporters Tuesday that the 49ers anticipate Bosa to return from a calf injury after the team's Week 8 bye. Bosa hasn't played since injuring his calf in practice prior to Week 3. San Francisco now expects to come out of the bye to face the Las Vegas Raiders in Week 9 with Buckner and Bosa on its defensive line. Another move out of Indy after post-Chris Ballard The trade of Buckner continues a roster purge in Indianapolis on the heels of last week's dismissal of general manager Chris Ballard . After moving guard Quenton Nelson to the Seattle Seahawks earlier Tuesday, Colts interim general manager Ed Dodds is continuing to stockpile draft picks in order to rebuild the roster. The two trades have netted the Colts third- and fourth-round picks in 2027 and a fifth-round selection in 2028. A 2-5 record and three straight losses have put the organization in a position to wave the white flag and look toward 2027. Buckner expressed his frustration with the Colts' lack of success this season following the Week 7 loss to the Minnesota Vikings. That came a week after saying , "I'm sick and tired of the same song and dance every year," after losing to the previously winless Tennessee Titans. Buckner, 32, is in the final year of his contract and, after receiving a $10 million roster bonus in March, is still owed a little under $8 million for the rest of the season. He carries a $26.6 million salary cap hit, which will leave $10.8 million in dead money on the Colts' books, according to Over the Cap . If he wasn't moved before the Nov. 10 NFL trade deadline, he was all but certain to leave in free agency.

stories.detailText: MINNEAPOLIS, MN - AUGUST 16: Minnesota Vikings defensive tackle Taki Taimani (94) looks on during the NFL preseason game between the New England Patriots and Minnesota Vikings on August 16th, 2025, in Minneapolis, MN. (Photo by Bailey Hillesheim/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Last week, the Detroit Lions hosted free agent nose tackle Taki Taimani for a visit. On Tuesday, they announced that Taimani has signed to their practice squad. To make room, the Lions released wide receiver Lawrence Keys from the practice squad. Taimani first entered the league in 2024 as an undrafted free agent out of Oregon. He was signed by the Minnesota Vikings and even made their initial 53-man roster in his rookie season. He played in seven games that year (70 total defensive snaps, 34 special teams) before an ankle injury landed him on injured reserve for the final 10 games. The following year, Taimani spent most of the season on the Vikings’ practice squad, seeing the call up for just two games in the 2025 season. This past year, he was waived with an injury designation late in training camp, and was released from the team’s injured reserve list in mid-September. Taimani is a big man, last listed at 6-foot-1, 324 pounds. In his brief appearances in game for the Vikings, he played multiple defensive tackle spots, including nose tackle. Prior to his time in the NFL, he was praised for his strength and anchoring ability as a two-gapper. Detroit doesn’t have a ton of run-stuffing defensive tackles on their roster outside of Alim McNeill and Tyleik Williams, although they did re-sign rookie Aidan Keanaaina to the practice squad last week. More interestingly, the Lions play the Vikings this week. So can Taimani help Detroit prepare for their second straight divisional home game?

stories.title: What on earth happened to this Eagles defense?
stories.summary: The Eagles defense was supposed to be loaded with stars. They’ve been duds thus far.
stories.detailText: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - OCTOBER 26: George Pickens #3 of the Dallas Cowboys catches a touchdown pass against Andrew Mukuba #24 of the Philadelphia Eagles during the second quarter at Lincoln Financial Field on October 26, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images We all knew the offense was going to be problematic. Sean Mannion’s new scheme would take time to get on its feet. Jalen Hurts would need to acclimate himself to it, the offensive line’s health was a question mark, and there didn’t appear to be many great answers at wide receiver. The prevailing wisdom was, if the Eagles were going to survive some early season growing pains from the offense, the defense would have to do a little more. But after so much offensive futility over the first six weeks, Hurts’ season ending blood clots, being forced to spend more time on the field than almost any other defense in the NFL and lugging around a 2-4 record, it appeared as if the effort dam broke for Vic Fangio’s unit in the Eagles’ embarrassing 38-21 loss to the Cowboys on Monday Night Football. Ironically, the offense actually showed a pulse for the first time all season. Tanner McKee is a backup quarterback for a reason, but he played pretty well through three quarters. After a really nice touchdown drive coming out of halftime gave the Eagles a 21-20 lead, the defense offered about as much resistance as single-ply Dollar Store toilet paper. It’s fair to say the defense has been far more disappointing than the offense through seven ugly weeks of football. Worse yet, it sure looked like they gave up on Monday night. Former Cowboys coach Wade Phillips summed it up best on ESPN’s Manning Cast. The numbers are disgusting, especially for a unit with this much high-priced, and soon-to-be high priced, talent on it. They have given up the 6th-most yards per game (371.3), 7th-most passing yards per game (239.9), and 6th-most rushing yards per game (131.4). That they are only 12th-worst in points per game allowed (25.0) is a bit of a miracle, thanks to a couple key goal line stands against Jacksonville and the Rams. They have a mere three interceptions and are the only team in the league without a fumble recovery. Those three total takeaways are tied with the Colts for fewest in the league. The Eagles’ 28.1% pressure rate is 10th-worst, they have the 9th-fewest total pressures, and are 2nd-worst in sacks per game (1.1). What’s worse, there are no injury excuses on the defensive side of the ball, certainly not against Dallas. While they missed Nolan Smith (concussion) on the edge rushing the passer, there was more than enough there to hold down the fort. Jalyx Hunt and Jonathan Greenard returned to the lineup, joining a group of tackles thought to be the best trio in the NFL. Instead, a Dallas running game that ranked 30th in the league coming into the Linc, ran for 204 yards on 38 carries, a 5.37 yard per carry average. Dak Prescott not only wasn’t sacked, he wasn’t even threatened. Bear in mind, this is a defensive line with Greenard ($25.2), Jalen Carter ($24.4) and Jordan Davis ($20.5) making a combined $70.1 million this season. Carter has 3 sacks and 18 tackles in seven games. Greenard has one tackle and one QB hit in four games. Davis has 27 tackles and 0.5 sacks. Remember Jalyx Hunt, the guy everyone swore up and down was due for a monster season and huge contract based off his summer reps? He remains without a sack and has 4 QB hits and 17 tackles. The other up-and-comer, Moro Ojomo, has no sacks, 3 QB hits and 18 tackles. They’re not exactly playing themselves into big money deals. Only Smith has shown up this, leading all team edge rushers with 3 sacks, 3 QB hits and 4 tackles for loss. Zack Baun and Quinyon Mitchell continue to play well, but the middle of the defense is missing safety Reed Blankenship’s steady play and Nakobe Dean’s athleticism and team leadership. Jeremiah Trotter, Jr. is now splitting time with last year’s first round pick, Jihaad Campbell, who has disappointed in a larger role this season. The safeties have been a disaster, and Riq Woolen has been extremely uneven. The decline in play from slot corner Cooper DeJean is particularly startling. He’s likely to get a big money extension at some point, but he’s putting it in jeopardy as he has suddenly begun missing a ton of tackles and finding himself at the center of defensive miscommunications that have led to big plays over the last few weeks. Part of the problem is how much Fangio’s unit has been on the field. Through their first seven games, the Eagles’ defense has been on the field for 67.3 plays per game, 4th-most in the NFL. That’s due to the offense leading the league in 3-and-outs. The defense has been on the field an average time of possession of 32:19. Only the Titans’ defense has been out on the field longer. However, on Monday night, the offense was holding its own. They gave the defense a shot to keep them in the game, but they couldn’t keep up with Prescott and the Dallas offense. It was too much to ask. It shouldn’t have been. The defensive side of the ball is where all the money is. So now, at 2-5, the Eagles’ season is likely over. Even in a weak NFC East, it’s clear they don’t have the horses on offense, and it’s clear something is amiss defensively. Howie Roseman should be a seller at the trade deadline in two weeks. At that time, it’s possible some of these contributors on defense will be playing somewhere else. For now, it’s one of the most disappointing performances by any Eagles unit in recent memory.

(Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year, we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bears fans and fans across the country. It’s only been two games, but Chicago Bears nickelback Kyler Gordon is showing exactly why defensive coordinator Dennis Allen talked him up so much when he was hired in 2025. Allen loves giving offenses plenty to think about pre-snap, and Gordon’s versatility lets Allen line him up anywhere. In Gordon’s two games this year, he has already set a career high in sacks (4), forced fumbles (2), and tackles for loss (5). It’s a small sample size with just 48 defensive snaps, but he’s only allowed 2 receptions in coverage for 5 yards. Various injuries limited Gordon to just 3 regular-season games last year, but the Bears won all three. Maybe it’s a coincidence, but in those three wins, the Bears defense gave up an average of 300 yards and 17.6 points, far below their season averages of 362 and 24.4. Gordon has already blitzed 10 times this season, but he may be asked to cover more in their next game against the Seattle Seahawks and wideout Jaxon Smith-Njigba, who does a lot of work out of the slot. Since coming off the PUP list, Kyler played 26 total snaps in his first game and 35 snaps in his second, so we could see that pushed closer to 50 on Monday night. stories.title: Cowboys at Eagles: The good, the bad, and ugly from Week 7
stories.summary: The Cowboys took a positive step forward this week.
stories.detailText: Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images In what was a must-win game, it was good to see the Dallas Cowboys take care of business in prime time on Monday Night Football to secure the 38-21 victory over their division rival, the Philadelphia Eagles. They now have a chance to string some wins together over the next few weeks and hopefully continue to get better. While it was good to see the Cowboys secure the win in the first of two matchups with the Eagles this year, it was also obvious this team still has a lot to work on. There seemed to be more positives than negatives this week, which is a good sign things could be heading in the right direction. Hopefully that continues. THE GOOD – RB Javonte Williams For the first time this season the Cowboys leaned heavily on the running game and it paid off in a big way. Dallas rushed for over 200 yards, but it was Javonte Williams who led the way, rushing for 155 yards and one touchdown on 25 carries. This is the first time this season No. 33 rushed for 100+ yards, averaging an impressive 6.2 yards per carry. If this continues Dallas’ offense can get back on track and become lethal once again. THE BAD – Cowboys’ defense The Cowboys defense is still a major concern. They faced a shorthanded Eagles offense without their starting QB and their top two receivers and still allowed Philadelphia to put up 21 points on them. And, had Saquon Barkley been a 100%, the outcome of this game may have been different. He alone managed to rush for 62 yards and a TD on just seven carries. Christian Parker still is a lot of work on before his defense isn’t considered such a liability. THE UGLY – Eagles’ defensive line The Cowboys offensive line has been criticized in the first six weeks of the season. Considering the talent they have across the board, they had been underperforming and it has negatively impacted the offensive production. On Monday night against the Eagles they looked much improved. They provided a clean pocket for Dak Prescott to throw from the and opened up huge holes for Javonte Williams to run through. The Cowboys gave up zero sacks and zero tackles for loss in the game. Jalen Carter and Jordan Davis were non-factors. The offensive line made Philadelphia’s defensive line look ugly.

stories.title: Chiefs-Seahawks: 5 stats to know from Week 7 loss
stories.summary: The notable statistics from Week 7 for Kansas City.
stories.detailText: (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images) | Getty Images Numbers never lie, right? There are so many statistics to parse through during the NFL season that some can be misleading. After each game, it’s a good exercise to review NFL “Next Gen Stats” and “Premium Stats” from Pro Football Focus and find the numbers that paint a picture not only of the game, but of what to expect from the Kansas City Chiefs moving forward. Here are three statistics from the Week 7 win over the Seattle Seahawks and what they could mean for the rest of the season: 1. L’Jarius Sneed was targeted on 55% of his snaps in pass coverage According to NFL Next Gen Stats , Sneed was in coverage for only 11 snaps, but the Seahawks threw six passes his way and completed five for 83 yards. He allowed a passer rating of 118.8 despite a season-low average yards of separation (1.5) on his throws. It was similar to Week 2 against the Indianapolis Colts , when Sneed was targeted on 56% of his coverage snaps and allowed 121 yards on 10 catches. In Seattle, it seemed as if defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo adjusted by keeping Sneed on the sideline more as the game went on, but high-end receivers will continue to be targeted heavily if Sneed is matched up on them from the slot. 2. The Chiefs ran a season-low 12 plays from under center Kansas City ran it five times and passed it seven times to gain 51 yards from under center against the Seahawks. Coming into the game, the team had called at least 21 under-center plays in each game and run the ball at least 11 times. The Chiefs totaled 100 fewer under-center yards than the second-lowest total this season (151 against the Colts). The offensive switchup, which made the unit look eerily similar to its 2025 version, may have been a preference for quarterback Patrick Mahomes after right tackle Jaylon Moore (concussion) was unable to play; it’s speculation, but under-center plays make the quarterback have to turn his back to the defense, and it may have been hard to trust that in this specific matchup. If Kansas City wants to get back on track, this can’t become a trend. 3. Ashton Gillotte registered 4 Stops in 28 run-defense snaps Translation: Gillotte kicked ass when he was on the field Stops, according to Pro Football Focus , are tackles that constitute a failure for the offense based on down and distance. Only linebacker Drue Tranquill (5) had more than Gillotte among the Chiefs’ defense in Seattle, and Gillotte’s tackles came only against handoffs. Ashton Gillotte is a big part of the Chiefs' solid early-down defense. He finds the ball. 4 'Stops' (PFF) was 2nd on the team despite not starting The whole DL kicked ass against the run and set up 3rd-and-longs vs. Seattle, who just traded for Quenton Nelson pic.twitter.com/NWMk3ohcKM — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) October 27, 2026 It highlights the role Gillotte has settled into after a plantar fascia injury during training camp disrupted his start to the season. He is a strong, high-effort run defender who finds the ball and gets the ball carrier on the ground. That was on full display against the Seahawks, helping the Chiefs get to favorable third-and-long situations. Nose tackle Khiyirs Tonga (3 Stops in 27 run-defense snaps) was also a key factor there. There’s little to be critical about when talking about Kansas City’s run defense. 4. Patrick Mahomes was pressured on 39% of his dropbacks 38.9% is the second-highest mark of his season, behind the Week 4 win over the Las Vegas Raiders , but Mahomes overcame it in Las Vegas, throwing for 225 yards and two touchdowns with a 97.2 passer rating. In Seattle, it was 165 yards and two turnover-worthy plays. You have to tip your cap sometimes; the Seattle defense is very good. However, the offense will struggle if the run game is bottled up and Mahomes faces pressure on more than 1/3 of his dropbacks. Outside of Jaylon Moore’s return, there isn’t much else the Chiefs can do to consistently provide clean pockets on obvious pass downs, so the run game has to keep them out of those spots. 5. The average Patrick Mahomes throw from a clean pocket traveled 3.6 yards downfield Mahomes was kept clean 47% of the time he dropped back against Seattle, a very low number that speaks to the constant pressure he dealt with, but even when he was protected, he rarely found a downfield throw to make. He checked it down to a running back often because of this; overall, the offensive scheme didn’t manufacture anything downfield against a very good Seattle defense.

stories.title: Who were the Titans’ 5 best players vs. Browns in Week 7?
stories.summary: Identifying the five best players from the Tennessee Titans’ Week 7 loss to the Cleveland Browns
stories.detailText: NASHVILLE, TENNESSEE - SEPTEMBER 20: Carnell Tate #14 of the Tennessee Titans warms up prior to the game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Nissan Stadium on September 20, 2026 in Nashville, Tennessee. (Photo by Johnnie Izquierdo/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Tennessee Titans were defeated 27-24 by the Cleveland Browns in Week 7 . It was a disappointing loss in true heartbreak fashion, as the Browns emerged victorious via a walkoff field goal. It was a competitive showing by an improving Titans squad. We’ve identified five+ talented players who performed admirably versus the Browns. Tony Pollard, RB Veteran running back Tony Pollard had one of the better days of his career . Pollard rushed for 129 yards and three touchdowns while averaging an effective 5.2 yards per attempt. The experienced ball-carrier consistently exposed creases for impactful gains against a stout Browns front seven. Offensive Line (Collectively) The offensive line deserves appreciation for how they generated those running lanes for Pollard. Furthermore, quarterback Cam Ward was sacked just once in protection. The run-blocking tape is an absolute joy to watch. Guys like JC Latham and Peter Skoronski continue to play high-level ball. Offensive line coach Carmen Bricillo has done a phenomenal job. Cor’Dale Flott, CB Cornerback Cor’Dale Flott is starting to play with confidence in Robert Saleh’s coverage scheme. He registered his second interception in as many games on Sunday. Flott’s interception versus the Colts was a picture-perfect example of playing zone coverage in Saleh’s scheme. The Deshaun Watson pick was a good play in man coverage. Carnell Tate, WR Rookie wide receiver Carnell Tate didn’t have a perfect afternoon. The fourth overall selection dropped a catchable pass from Cam Ward and also lost a keynote fumble on what would have been a sizable gain. Tate still had a strong showing, registering five receptions for 69 yards on a team-high seven targets. Anthony Hill Jr., LB Rookie linebacker Anthony Hill Jr. continues being a total revelation for the defense. The former Texas Longhorns standout finally forced his first turnover, stripping TE Harold Fannin Jr. of the football. Hill had another 12 total tackles versus the Browns, bringing his season-long total to 68.

teamStories.summary: After four straight losses, it’s time for Las Vegas Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak to tweak his approach on offense.
teamStories.detailText: (Photo by Candice Ward/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders played another team that was heavily hampered by injuries and got the crap kicked out of them again. From the second series, it was obvious to anyone with eyes that the defense had nothing for 13-personnel. Offensively, the flaws of Klint Kubiak’s rookie head coaching campaign were on full display. Kubiak continues to pick interesting times to be aggressive on fourth downs in the red zone with little to no return on his analytical beliefs. Combined with going for two-point conversions twice and failing to convert, his aggressiveness continues to cost the team points. Pressing is natural and to be expected when trying to come from behind, but when down by multiple scores, points in every possession are essential. Trying to win games in one possession is something he will need to calm down on. After seven weeks with the offensive lineup, Kubiak continues to trot out; his offense is entirely predictable. Former first-round draft pick and #6 overall Ashton Jeanty is more Jalen Richard than the generational talent he was billed as. Every time Mike Washington Jr. touches the football and clears the line of scrimmage, it is clear who is the better option at running back. To everyone except Kubiak, who continues to feature an ineffective runner for three plays and a punt. The Rams have run man coverage 53.3% of the time today so far vs. the Raiders, per Sumer Sports. That’s 29.8% higher than the league average of man usage. https://t.co/cvTOzs5aj1 — Jesse Merrick – Silver & Black Sports Network (@JesseSBSN) October 25, 2026 Brock Bowers, as a wide receiver, was a good experiment and can be effective in spurts, but as an every-down wideout, he’s not the answer. Bowers finished the game with six receptions for 73 yards, but despite these numbers, it was still a rather pedestrian game for him. Most of his catches were junk-time plays when the defense had eased off the press coverage. The fact that the Kubiak isn’t able to call plays where his receivers can beat man coverage is an indictment of not only his play calling but also his personnel. Beating man coverage is as elementary as football gets. But, it’s not all on the wide receivers. Cousins, for all the good that he has done and being tied for the league lead in passing touchdowns, hasn’t been hitting wide-open receivers when they have presented themselves. These are the plays that the rookie will let it rip and 9/10 going to be a TD. WAO, wide ass open. Kirk has done well but this can’t keep happening. https://t.co/syQtZSAYMf — Phil Robinson III (@PhilRobinsonIII) October 26, 2026 Finally some offense In the second half, speedy wide receiver Tre Tucker showed why he should be more than an afterthought in this offense. With a pass he could do something with, he showed YAC (yards after the catch) ability, taking a short reception and finishing with a 41-yard catch-and-run. Later, he added a 37-yard catch-and-run for a touchdown after making a man miss. Jeanty, had his lowest average yard per carry total of the season 1.9 yards, and is averaging 2.9 yards per carry on the season. However, he has proved his worth as a pass catcher. Catching a season-high eight passes on eight targets, including both a 22-yard sideline catch and a 15-yard touchdown pass. Ultimately, the offense was unable to overcome the lack of their own running game and Kubiak’s strange fascination with wanting to see Washington’s blocking ability over his 4.9 yards-per-carry average. On a team with a non-existent rushing attack, keeping a runner like Washington on the bench instead of switching Jeanty to a complementary role, which better suits him, is hurting the team. If “just win baby” is the goal, Kubiak needs to get over his own biases and coach to the strengths of his team and players.

headlines.title: Broncos win 30–16 over Cardinals
headlines.summary: Denver beat Arizona 30–16. Bo Nix threw for 222 yards and a touchdown on 15 of 29 passing and ran for another score on seven carries. RJ Harvey added two catches for 54 yards and a touchdown. For Arizona, Jacoby Brissett threw for 272 yards and a touchdown, and Trey McBride caught 10 passes for 111 yards and a score. Arizona will also be without receiver Jalen Brooks, who will have season-ending wrist surgery.

headlines.title: Harbaugh fires back at flag on Skattebo's helmet hit
headlines.summary: The Giants beat the Texans 27–21 on Sunday, but the talking point was a penalty. Cam Skattebo lowered his helmet into Texans safety M.J. Stewart on a 7-yard run, and was flagged for unnecessary roughness. The flag moved New York from second-and-3 at the 30 to first-and-20 at its own 13. Harbaugh argued with an official on the sideline and on Monday said the way Skattebo ran was "the way you're supposed to run".

headlines.title: Falcons upset unbeaten 49ers
headlines.summary: Atlanta beat San Francisco 29–20 and ended the 49ers' perfect start. The Falcons forced four turnovers and scored 13 points off them. Michael Penix Jr. completed 25 of 34 passes for 213 yards and three touchdowns, and Drake London had seven catches for 66 yards and a touchdown. Rookie linebacker Kendal Daniels had an interception and a fumble recovery, and his 29-yard return set up a field goal that gave Atlanta a two-possession lead. Christian McCaffrey left for much of the first half with a thigh injury, but the reports say it doesn't appear to be serious.

headlines.title: Bengals beat the Ravens without Lamar Jackson
headlines.summary: Cincinnati won 35–13 at Baltimore after a slow first half. Joe Burrow threw four touchdown passes in the second half and finished 22 of 30 for 292 yards. Tee Higgins had six catches for 148 yards and a touchdown. Jackson was sidelined with a left ankle sprain, and Tyler Huntley threw for 298 yards with one touchdown and one interception for Baltimore. It was the Ravens' second straight divisional loss.

headlines.title: Browns win again with a late drive, Titans drop to 1-6
headlines.summary: Cleveland beat Tennessee 27–24. Deshaun Watson led his fifth game-winning drive in the fourth quarter this season, connecting with Harold Fannin Jr. on a 36-yard catch-and-run before Andre Szmyt kicked a 32-yard field goal. Quinshon Judkins ran for 96 yards and two touchdowns, and KC Concepcion had eight catches for 129 yards. For Tennessee, Tony Pollard ran 25 times for 129 yards and three touchdowns, but it was the Titans' sixth loss of the season.

headlines.title: Giants beat Texans in overtime, Skattebo hurts hamstring
headlines.summary: New York beat Houston 27–21 in overtime. Cam Skattebo finished with 17 carries for 124 yards and a touchdown. In overtime he ran 42 yards to the Houston 30, and Devin Singletary scored on the next play. J.J. McCarthy completed 20 of 28 passes for 252 yards. Houston had tied the game late, and C.J. Stroud threw for 153 yards and two touchdowns. Skattebo told ESPN he 'felt something in his hamstring' on his final carry of the game.
